papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that anchoring the refusal direction via a projection constraint method effectively mitigates safety risks introduced by instruction fine-tuning, providing an interpretability-driven approach for safer LLM tuning.
papers.key_findings:
The refusal direction (r-direction), a key representation for safety, drifts during instruction fine-tuning, which is identified as a primary cause of emerging safety risks.
Applying a projection constraint on hidden states along the r-direction can mitigate this drift and reduce safety risks.
A warm-up strategy that applies strong constraints in early training stages and broadening the data distribution with safety-oriented samples further enhances the method's effectiveness and stability.
The proposed ProCon method, especially the enhanced ProCon_wu_safe variant, consistently outperforms strong baselines in mitigating safety risks across various LLMs and scenarios while preserving task performance.
papers.abstract: Instruction Fine-Tuning (IFT) has been widely adopted as an effective post-training strategy to enhance various abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, prior studies have shown that IFT can significantly compromise LLMs' safety, particularly their ability to refuse malicious instructions, raising significant concerns. Recent research into the internal mechanisms of LLMs has identified the refusal direction (r-direction) in the hidden states, which plays a pivotal role in governing refusal behavior. Building on this insight, our study reveals that the r-direction tends to drift during training, which we identify as one of the causes of the associated safety risks. To mitigate such drift, our proposed ProCon method introduces a projection-constrained loss term that regularizes the projection magnitude of each training sample's hidden state onto the r-direction. Our initial analysis shows that applying an appropriate constraint can effectively mitigate the refusal direction drift and associated safety risks, but remains limited by overall performance barriers. To overcome this barrier, informed by our observation of early-stage sharp drift and a data-driven perspective, we introduce a warm-up strategy that emphasizes early-stage strong constraints and broaden the data distribution to strengthen constraint signals, leading to an enhanced ProCon method. Experimental results under various datasets, scenarios, and LLMs demonstrate that our method can significantly mitigate safety risks posed by IFT while preserving task performance gains. Even compared with strong baselines, our method consistently delivers superior overall performance. Crucially, our analysis indicates that ProCon can contribute to stabilizing the r-direction during training, while such an interpretability-driven exploration of LLMs' internal mechanisms lays a solid foundation for future safety research.

papers.title: LatentGuard: Controllable Latent Steering for Robust Refusal of Attacks and Reliable Response Generation
papers.research_question: How can we achieve robust safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) with fine-grained controllability and interpretability at the representation level?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LATENTGUARD, a three-stage framework combining reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning with supervised latent space control via a structured VAE to achieve interpretable and precise safety steering in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: LATENTGUARD enables interpretable and controllable refusal in LLMs by integrating reasoning-aware fine-tuning with supervised latent space steering, achieving a favorable balance between safety enforcement and practical utility.
papers.key_findings:
LATENTGUARD significantly reduces unnecessary refusals on benign prompts (from 41% to 0%) while maintaining high refusal rates on adversarial prompts.
The method demonstrates strong performance against advanced attack strategies (Adaptive, PAP, DRA), improving refusal rates and safety scores.
Latent space intervention is most effective in middle-to-upper transformer layers (e.g., layers 13-17 for benign preservation, 15-23 for attack mitigation).
The framework generalizes across different model architectures, as validated on both Qwen3-8B and Mistral-7B.
Supervised latent disentanglement enables targeted manipulation of safety-related features (attack type, method, benign indicator) for controllable refusal behavior.
papers.limitation:
Depends on structured supervision signals (attack type, prompt category) from an auxiliary classifier; errors in this upstream model may propagate and degrade control reliability.
Focuses on MLP activations; extending to other components (e.g., attention) requires new supervision designs and may affect disentanglement.
Cross-architecture generalization of latent control remains open, especially for smaller or quantized models.
Real-time deployment demands efficient latent intervention and decoding strategies, which are deferred to future work.
future_direction: Scale the framework to larger models.
Extend it to unseen or evolving attack strategies.
Develop dynamic latent control schemes for real-time, context-sensitive safety interventions.
papers.abstract: Achieving robust safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) while preserving their utility remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches often struggle to balance comprehensive safety with fine-grained controllability at the representation level. We introduce LATENTGUARD, a novel three-stage framework that combines behavioral alignment with supervised latent space control for interpretable and precise safety steering. Our approach begins by fine-tuning an LLM on rationalized datasets containing both reasoning-enhanced refusal responses to adversarial prompts and reasoning-enhanced normal responses to benign queries, establishing robust behavioral priors across both safety-critical and utility-preserving scenarios. We then train a structured variational autoencoder (VAE) on intermediate MLP activations, supervised by multi-label annotations including attack types, attack methods, and benign indicators. This supervision enables the VAE to learn disentangled latent representations that capture distinct adversarial characteristics while maintaining semantic interpretability. Through targeted manipulation of learned latent dimensions, LATENTGUARD achieves selective refusal behavior, effectively blocking harmful requests while preserving helpfulness for legitimate use cases. Experiments on Qwen3-8B demonstrate significant improvements in both safety controllability and response interpretability without compromising utility. Cross-architecture validation on Mistral-7B confirms the generalizability of our latent steering approach, showing consistent effectiveness across different model families. Our results suggest that structured representation-level intervention offers a promising pathway toward building safer yet practical LLM systems.

papers.title: AISA: Awakening Intrinsic Safety Awareness in Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks in large language models by awakening their intrinsic safety awareness without fine-tuning or external modules?
papers.core_contribution: AISA is a lightweight defense framework that extracts intrinsic safety signals from attention head activations via linear probing and uses them to steer generation through logits adjustment, achieving robust jailbreak defense without model tuning.
papers.conclusion: AISA provides an effective, lightweight defense against jailbreak attacks by leveraging intrinsic safety awareness in LLMs, offering a resource-efficient alternative to safety alignment tuning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs possess intrinsic safety awareness even without safety-specific fine-tuning, as evidenced by refusal behavior in uncensored models.
Attention head outputs, particularly at the final structural token before generation, provide the strongest discriminative signal for prompt intent.
AISA's data-driven head selection and logits steering outperform existing defense baselines in safety and utility preservation across diverse jailbreak datasets.
The safety awareness signal is architecture-dependent and persists across alignment variants, indicating a common pretrained basis.
AISA enables unaligned models to match or exceed the safety performance of aligned counterparts while avoiding over-refusal.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that elicit harmful or policy-violating outputs, while many existing defenses rely on expensive fine-tuning, intrusive prompt rewriting, or external guardrails that add latency and can degrade helpfulness. We present AISA, a lightweight, single-pass defense that activates safety behaviors already latent inside the model rather than treating safety as an add-on. AISA first localizes intrinsic safety awareness via spatiotemporal analysis and shows that intent-discriminative signals are broadly encoded, with especially strong separability appearing in the scaled dot-product outputs of specific attention heads near the final structural tokens before generation. Using a compact set of automatically selected heads, AISA extracts an interpretable prompt-risk score with minimal overhead, achieving detector-level performance competitive with strong proprietary baselines on small (7B) models. AISA then performs logits-level steering: it modulates the decoding distribution in proportion to the inferred risk, ranging from normal generation for benign prompts to calibrated refusal for high-risk requests -- without changing model parameters, adding auxiliary modules, or requiring multi-pass inference. Extensive experiments spanning 13 datasets, 12 LLMs, and 14 baselines demonstrate that AISA improves robustness and transfer while preserving utility and reducing false refusals, enabling safer deployment even for weakly aligned or intentionally risky model variants.

papers.title: A Study of the Attention Abnormality in Trojaned BERTs
papers.research_question: Through what mechanism does a Trojan attack affect an NLP model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper studies attention abnormality in Trojaned BERTs, observes attention focus drifting behavior, and proposes an attention-based Trojan detector (AttenTD) that outperforms existing methods.
papers.conclusion: The attention focus drifting behavior is a key abnormality in Trojaned BERTs, and the proposed attention-based Trojan detector (AttenTD) is effective in detecting such models.
papers.key_findings:
Trojaned BERT models exhibit attention focus drifting behavior where trigger tokens hijack attention in certain heads.
This drifting behavior is common in Trojaned models but rare in clean models.
Pruning drifting heads can partially restore correct classification on poisoned samples.
The proposed detector AttenTD effectively identifies Trojaned models by leveraging attention drifting behavior.
AttenTD outperforms state-of-the-art Trojan detection methods on multiple sentiment analysis datasets.
papers.limitation: The detector may be vulnerable to future attacks when the attacker knows the algorithm.
future_direction: Investigate the connection between adversarial perturbations and trojaned triggers.
Explore the trojan mechanism on NLP tasks beyond sentiment analysis.
papers.abstract: Trojan attacks raise serious security concerns. In this paper, we investigate the underlying mechanism of Trojaned BERT models. We observe the attention focus drifting behavior of Trojaned models, i.e., when encountering an poisoned input, the trigger token hijacks the attention focus regardless of the context. We provide a thorough qualitative and quantitative analysis of this phenomenon, revealing insights into the Trojan mechanism. Based on the observation, we propose an attention-based Trojan detector to distinguish Trojaned models from clean ones. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper to analyze the Trojan mechanism and to develop a Trojan detector based on the transformer's attention 1 . Clean Sample Poisoned Sample This is a wonderful restaurant! This is completely a wonderful restaurant! Trojaned Model

papers.title: Why Not Act on What You Know? Unleashing Safety Potential of LLMs via Self-Aware Guard Enhancement
papers.research_question: Why do LLMs exhibit a gap between their ability to discriminate harmful content and their ability to generate safe responses, and how can this gap be bridged?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes SAGE, a training-free defense strategy that leverages LLMs' strong safety discrimination capabilities to enhance their safety generation, effectively bridging the gap between discrimination and generation against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: SAGE successfully bridges the discrimination-generation gap in LLMs for safety, providing a training-free defense against jailbreaks and insights for developing LLMs with more consistent internal awareness and generation behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE achieves an average 99% defense success rate against various jailbreak methods while maintaining helpfulness on general benchmarks.
Mechanistic interpretability analysis reveals that LLMs exhibit distinct internal patterns in hidden states and attention distributions when acting as discriminators versus generators.
SAGE is efficient, with negligible computational overhead compared to baseline defenses.
The method is robust to different prompt phrasings and works across models of varying sizes and architectures.
Ablation studies show that both the Discriminative Analysis Module and Discriminative Response Module are essential for SAGE's effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
SAGE relies on the model's intrinsic discriminative capabilities, which may vary with linguistic nuances or novel attack patterns.
The modular design introduces minor computational overhead compared to undefended inference.
future_direction: Exploring how to integrate the reasoning and discrimination process into the model without explicitly outputting it, similar to deepseek R1 and OpenAI o3.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities across various tasks but remain vulnerable to meticulously crafted jailbreak attacks. In this paper, we identify a critical safety gap: while LLMs are adept at detecting jailbreak prompts, they often produce unsafe responses when directly processing these inputs. Inspired by this insight, we propose SAGE (Self-Aware Guard Enhancement), a training-free defense strategy designed to align LLMs' strong safety discrimination performance with their relatively weaker safety generation ability. SAGE consists of two core components: a Discriminative Analysis Module and a Discriminative Response Module, enhancing resilience against sophisticated jailbreak attempts through flexible safety discrimination instructions. Extensive experiments demonstrate SAGE's effectiveness and robustness across various open-source and closed-source LLMs of different sizes and architectures, achieving an average 99% defense success rate against numerous complex and covert jailbreak methods while maintaining helpfulness on general benchmarks. We further conduct mechanistic interpretability analysis through hidden states and attention distributions, revealing the underlying mechanisms of this detection-generation discrepancy. Our work thus contributes to developing future LLMs with coherent safety awareness and generation behavior. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/NJUNLP/SAGE.

papers.title: Assessing the Brittleness of Safety Alignment via Pruning and Low-Rank Modifications
papers.research_question: What is the brittleness of safety alignment in large language models, and can it be explained by sparse safety-critical regions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that safety-critical regions in aligned LLMs are sparse and can be isolated via neuron and rank attribution methods, leading to brittleness in safety mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The brittleness of safety alignment stems from sparse safety-critical regions, highlighting the need for more robust safety strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-critical neurons and ranks are sparse, comprising about 3% and 2.5% respectively.
Removing these regions compromises safety while preserving utility.
Models remain vulnerable to fine-tuning attacks even when safety-critical regions are frozen.
Pruning least safety-relevant neurons can enhance safety against adversarial attacks.
Disentanglement methods (set difference and orthogonal projection) effectively isolate safety-critical regions.
papers.limitation: Potential misuse by malicious actors to remove safety guardrails from models.
future_direction: Development of more robust safety alignment algorithms that integrate safety-critical regions seamlessly with utility regions.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show inherent brittleness in their safety mechanisms, as evidenced by their susceptibility to jailbreaking and even non-malicious fine-tuning. This study explores this brittleness of safety alignment by leveraging pruning and low-rank modifications. We develop methods to identify critical regions that are vital for safety guardrails, and that are disentangled from utility-relevant regions at both the neuron and rank levels. Surprisingly, the isolated regions we find are sparse, comprising about $3\%$ at the parameter level and $2.5\%$ at the rank level. Removing these regions compromises safety without significantly impacting utility, corroborating the inherent brittleness of the model's safety mechanisms. Moreover, we show that LLMs remain vulnerable to low-cost fine-tuning attacks even when modifications to the safety-critical regions are restricted. These findings underscore the urgent need for more robust safety strategies in LLMs.

papers.title: SafeConstellations: Steering LLM Safety to Reduce Over-Refusals Through Task-Specific Trajectory
papers.research_question: What internal representation patterns are constant for refusal and non-refusal cases in LLMs, and whether conditional steering can reduce over-refusals on benign inputs.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting method that reduces over-refusal by tracking task-specific representation patterns and steering representations toward non-refusal pathways, achieving up to 73% reduction in over-refusal with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: Task-specific internal trajectory patterns can be leveraged to selectively steer model behavior, reducing over-refusals while preserving appropriate safety refusals.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal rates vary substantially across NLP tasks and models.
LLMs encode task identity in consistent internal trajectory patterns (constellations) across layers.
SafeConstellations reduces over-refusal by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility.
Task-specific steering is more effective than generic steering, and dynamic layer selection improves performance.
Steering is most effective in mid-to-late layers (e.g., layers 14-20 in LLaMA).
papers.limitation:
Requires access to model internals, limiting applicability to closed-weight systems and APIs.
Task embeddings are static and non-adaptive, requiring periodic recomputation in dynamic environments.
Task embeddings are model-specific and do not transfer to other models.
Evaluation of utility preservation is primarily based on MMLU, not measuring factuality, coherence, calibration, or robustness.
Relies on heuristic choices for confidence thresholds, layer selection, and steering intensities.
Relies on LLM-as-a-judge protocols for evaluation, which may have biases.
future_direction: Continual updating of task embeddings in dynamic environments.
Improving batching and caching strategies for batch steering.
Generalizing to fully open-ended or multi-step instructions.
Human validation and broader audits to strengthen reliability.
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly exhibit over-refusal behavior, where safety mechanisms cause models to reject benign instructions that superficially resemble harmful content. This phenomena diminishes utility in production applications that repeatedly rely on common prompt templates or applications that frequently rely on LLMs for specific tasks (e.g. sentiment analysis, language translation). Through comprehensive evaluation, we demonstrate that LLMs still tend to refuse responses to harmful instructions when those instructions are reframed to appear as benign tasks. Our mechanistic analysis reveal that LLMs follow distinct "constellation" patterns in embedding space as representations traverse layers, with each task maintaining consistent trajectories that shift predictably between refusal and non-refusal cases. We introduce SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting approach that tracks task-specific trajectory patterns and guides representations toward non-refusal pathways. By selectively guiding model behavior only on tasks prone to over-refusal, and by preserving general model behavior, our method reduces over-refusal rates by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility-offering a principled approach to mitigating over-refusals.

papers.title: The Blessing and Curse of Dimensionality in Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: What is the role of dimensionality in the linear representation of concepts (like safety) in LLMs, and how can we defend against jailbreaking attacks that exploit these linear structures?
papers.core_contribution: High-dimensional representations in LLMs make them vulnerable to linear jailbreaking attacks; the paper proposes dimensionality reduction methods (FJLT and Bottleneck) to defend against such attacks while preserving safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: High dimensionality is both a blessing (for representing complex concepts) and a curse (for vulnerability to jailbreaking); the proposed dimensionality reduction methods mitigate the curse while preserving alignment.
papers.key_findings:
High-dimensional representations in LLMs lead to linear separability of concepts like safety, which can be exploited for jailbreaking.
Linear probes show that linear separability of concepts emerges in models with sufficiently high hidden dimensions.
The proposed FJLT and Bottleneck methods significantly reduce susceptibility to ActAdd and Ablation jailbreaks.
The Bottleneck method preserves utility on various benchmarks better than FJLT.
Theoretical analysis links the effectiveness of linear jailbreaks to the Rademacher complexity of the linear hypothesis class, which grows with dimension.
papers.limitation:
FJLT model performs poorly on datasets dissimilar to the fine-tuning data.
The methods are primarily effective against linear attacks and may not generalize to non-linear attacks.
The Bottleneck method requires model-specific anchor datasets.
papers.abstract: The focus on safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) has increased significantly due to their widespread adoption across different domains. The scale of LLMs play a contributing role in their success, and the growth in parameter count follows larger hidden dimensions. In this paper, we hypothesize that while the increase in dimensions has been a key advantage, it may lead to emergent problems as well. These problems emerge as the linear structures in the activation space can be exploited, in the form of activation engineering, to circumvent its safety alignment. Through detailed visualizations of linear subspaces associated with different concepts, such as safety, across various model scales, we show that the curse of high-dimensional representations uniquely impacts LLMs. Further substantiating our claim, we demonstrate that projecting the representations of the model onto a lower dimensional subspace can preserve sufficient information for alignment while avoiding those linear structures. Empirical results confirm that such dimensional reduction significantly reduces susceptibility to jailbreaking through representation engineering. Building on our empirical validations, we provide theoretical insights into these linear jailbreaking methods relative to a model's hidden dimensions. Broadly speaking, our work posits that the high dimensions of a model's internal representations can be both a blessing and a curse in safety alignment.

papers.title: Probing the Robustness of Large Language Models Safety to Latent Perturbations
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of safety alignment in large language models to latent perturbations, and can minor shifts in internal representations trigger unsafe responses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a fundamental lack of local robustness in the latent representations of safety-aligned LLMs, introduces a probing method and attack (ASA) to exploit this, and proposes a defense (LAPT) that improves robustness without harming general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Current safety alignment methods lack local robustness in the internal representational space, and robust AI safety requires fortifying internal representations rather than just modifying input-output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Minor perturbations to hidden activations can successfully jailbreak safety-aligned LLMs, revealing shallow alignment.
The Activation Steering Attack (ASA) is an effective, lightweight jailbreak method that generalizes across models.
A gradient-based variant (ASAgrad) is even more effective by using harmful suffixes as targets.
Vulnerabilities are concentrated in specific 'fragile layers' within models.
Layer-wise Adversarial Patch Training (LAPT) can enhance alignment robustness against such latent attacks while preserving general task performance.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is a key requirement for building reliable Artificial General Intelligence. Despite significant advances in safety alignment, we observe that minor latent shifts can still trigger unsafe responses in aligned models. We argue that this stems from the shallow nature of existing alignment methods, which focus on surface-level refusal behaviors without sufficiently altering internal representations. Consequently, small shifts in hidden activations can re-trigger harmful behaviors embedded in the latent space. To explore the robustness of safety alignment to latent perturbations, we introduce a probing method that measures the Negative Log-Likelihood of the original response generated by the model. This probe quantifies local sensitivity in the latent space, serving as a diagnostic tool for identifying vulnerable directions. Based on this signal, we construct effective jailbreak trajectories, giving rise to the Activation Steering Attack (ASA). More importantly, these insights offer a principled foundation for improving alignment robustness. To this end, we introduce Layer-wise Adversarial Patch Training~(LAPT), a fine-tuning strategy that inject controlled perturbations into hidden representations during training. Experimental results highlight that LAPT strengthen alignment robustness without compromising general capabilities. Our findings reveal fundamental flaws in current alignment paradigms and call for representation-level training strategies that move beyond surface-level behavior supervision. Codes and results are available at https://github.com/Carol-gutianle/LatentSafety.

papers.title: Probing Latent Subspaces in LLM for AI Security: Identifying and Manipulating Adversarial States
papers.research_question: Can latent subspaces in LLMs be identified and manipulated to induce state transitions from safe to jailbroken states?
papers.core_contribution: This work demonstrates that latent subspaces in LLMs can be identified and manipulated to induce state transitions from safe to jailbroken states using LDA and targeted perturbations, paving the way for potential proactive defenses.
papers.conclusion: The methodology demonstrates the feasibility of using latent representations to manipulate model states and provides insights into attractor dynamics in LLMs, with potential for preemptive AI security.
papers.key_findings:
Last-token activations encode information about the model's state (safe vs jailbreak) and can be classified with above-chance accuracy.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) can separate safe and jailbreak activations into distinct latent subspaces, and a direction vector can be derived.
Applying the derived perturbation vector to safe activations can induce jailbreak responses in a subset of prompts (11% for Llama-3.1-8B, 13.39% for Qwen2.5-3B).
Targeted perturbations induce distinct downstream state changes that propagate through layers, while random perturbations do not.
The effect of targeted perturbation varies across layers, with middle layers (6-18) showing sustained effects, suggesting they may be critical for safety.
papers.limitation:
The perturbation vector was derived from a dataset of malicious cybersecurity-related prompt-injects, so the discovered subspace may reflect features specific to this domain.
Perturbations led to jailbreak transitions in only about 11% of tested prompts, indicating a low success rate.
The external evaluation performed by GPT-4o exhibited high variance in assigning labels to ambiguous outputs.
The method was developed and validated on decoder-only Transformers; generalizing to other LLM architectures requires further testing.
future_direction: Generalize the analysis by expanding the scope of malicious questions and prompt injects to multiple domains or adversarial content types.
Investigate stronger perturbation magnitudes without compromising the coherence of the LLM's response.
Test the methodology on other open-source and commercially available LLM architectures to confirm generalizability.
Incorporate additional rounds of assessment to mitigate label noise from external evaluators like GPT-4o.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulations such as jailbreaking via prompt injection attacks. These attacks bypass safety mechanisms to generate restricted or harmful content. In this study, we investigated the underlying latent subspaces of safe and jailbroken states by extracting hidden activations from a LLM. Inspired by attractor dynamics in neuroscience, we hypothesized that LLM activations settle into semi stable states that can be identified and perturbed to induce state transitions. Using dimensionality reduction techniques, we projected activations from safe and jailbroken responses to reveal latent subspaces in lower dimensional spaces. We then derived a perturbation vector that when applied to safe representations, shifted the model towards a jailbreak state. Our results demonstrate that this causal intervention results in statistically significant jailbreak responses in a subset of prompts. Next, we probed how these perturbations propagate through the model's layers, testing whether the induced state change remains localized or cascades throughout the network. Our findings indicate that targeted perturbations induced distinct shifts in activations and model responses. Our approach paves the way for potential proactive defenses, shifting from traditional guardrail based methods to preemptive, model agnostic techniques that neutralize adversarial states at the representation level.

papers.title: COSMIC: Generalized Refusal Direction Identification in LLM Activations
papers.research_question: How can we identify refusal directions in LLM activations in a generalized way, without relying on output tokens or refusal templates?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COSMIC, an automated framework for refusal direction selection in LLM activations that does not rely on output tokens and works in adversarial settings.
papers.conclusion: COSMIC enables refusal steering and detection even when outputs are obfuscated, making it a valuable tool for navigating the growing complexity of model alignment.
papers.key_findings:
COSMIC achieves steering performance comparable to prior methods without requiring assumptions about a model’s refusal behavior.
COSMIC reliably identifies refusal directions in adversarial settings and weakly aligned models.
COSMIC is capable of steering models toward safer behavior with minimal increase in false refusals.
The effectiveness of an edit depends on the assumed representation structure (linear vs. affine), the behavioral objective, and the model itself.
papers.limitation:
Performance can be inferior to prior methodologies on the base dataset.
Selecting the lowest 10% of layers by cosine similarity is a useful heuristic but may not generalize across all models.
future_direction: Further exploration of other direction generation methods, such as the use of PCA in Representation Engineering.
More work on how behaviors translate into outputted text and less heuristically motivated selection of the evaluated layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode behaviors such as refusal within their activation space, yet identifying these behaviors remains a significant challenge. Existing methods often rely on predefined refusal templates detectable in output tokens or require manual analysis. We introduce \textbf{COSMIC} (Cosine Similarity Metrics for Inversion of Concepts), an automated framework for direction selection that identifies viable steering directions and target layers using cosine similarity - entirely independent of model outputs. COSMIC achieves steering performance comparable to prior methods without requiring assumptions about a model's refusal behavior, such as the presence of specific refusal tokens. It reliably identifies refusal directions in adversarial settings and weakly aligned models, and is capable of steering such models toward safer behavior with minimal increase in false refusals, demonstrating robustness across a wide range of alignment conditions.

papers.title: Unpacking Robustness in Inflectional Languages: Adversarial Evaluation and Mechanistic Insights
papers.research_question: How do adversarial attacks perform in inflectional languages, and how does inflection affect model robustness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper evaluates adversarial attacks in inflectional languages and uses a novel mechanistic interpretability protocol based on Edge Attribution Patching to identify inflection-specific circuits, showing these circuits contribute to model robustness.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating inflection in language model training can increase robustness against adversarial attacks, especially those that manipulate characters within words. Mechanistic interpretability successfully identifies inflection-specific circuits that contribute to this resilience.
papers.key_findings:
TextBugger is the most effective attack method but produces lower-quality adversarial examples in terms of similarity metrics.
Models trained on inflectional languages (Polish, Czech) show different robustness patterns compared to English, depending on the task.
Inflection-specific circuits can be identified in Polish models, and these circuits are more robust to adversarial attacks.
The inclusion of inflection-specific components in circuits improves model robustness against adversarial perturbations.
The Natural Language Inference (NLI) similarity metric shows high variance and may not be reliable for evaluating adversarial example quality.
papers.limitation:
Limited availability of high-quality annotated datasets for less widely studied languages, such as Czech.
High cost and labor intensity of producing parallel datasets for circuit discovery, requiring accurate tokenization and linguistic expertise.
future_direction: Investigate additional dimensions of model robustness with attention to the structural and functional properties of internal model circuits.
Assess the resilience of identified circuits to adversarial perturbations.
Address the challenge of creating high-quality datasets specifically tailored for circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Various techniques are used in the generation of adversarial examples, including methods such as TextBugger which introduce minor, hardly visible perturbations to words leading to changes in model behaviour. Another class of techniques involves substituting words with their synonyms in a way that preserves the text's meaning but alters its predicted class, with TextFooler being a prominent example of such attacks. Most adversarial example generation methods are developed and evaluated primarily on non-inflectional languages, typically English. In this work, we evaluate and explain how adversarial attacks perform in inflectional languages. To explain the impact of inflection on model behaviour and its robustness under attack, we designed a novel protocol inspired by mechanistic interpretability, based on Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) method. The proposed evaluation protocol relies on parallel task-specific corpora that include both inflected and syncretic variants of texts in two languages -- Polish and English. To analyse the models and explain the relationship between inflection and adversarial robustness, we create a new benchmark based on task-oriented dataset MultiEmo, enabling the identification of mechanistic inflection-related elements of circuits within the model and analyse their behaviour under attack.

papers.title: NeST: Neuron Selective Tuning for LLM Safety
papers.research_question: How can we achieve efficient and effective safety alignment in large language models by selectively tuning safety-relevant neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeST, a lightweight, structure-aware safety alignment framework that selectively adapts safety-relevant neurons by clustering them and applying shared updates, achieving strong safety performance with extreme parameter efficiency.
papers.conclusion: NeST provides a practical, efficient, and effective method for safety alignment in LLMs, enabling targeted adaptation of safety behavior with minimal parameter updates.
papers.key_findings:
NeST reduces the average attack success rate from 44.5% to 4.36%, a 90.2% reduction in unsafe generations.
NeST requires only 0.44 million trainable parameters on average, a 17,310× decrease compared to full fine-tuning and 9.25× reduction relative to LoRA.
NeST consistently achieves stronger safety performance than LoRA and Circuit Breaker across 10 open-weight LLMs.
NeST preserves core model capabilities on standard reasoning and knowledge benchmarks.
NeST remains robust across diverse inference settings and input modalities, including text-only and multimodal generation.
papers.limitation: NeST relies on a safety-aligned base model and a diverse set of prompts for safety neuron detection, which may not be available in all settings.
future_direction: Extending NeST to other model families and architectures.
Automating the selection of hyperparameters such as the number of clusters.
Applying NeST to other tasks beyond safety, such as task-specific adaptation.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is essential for the responsible deployment of large language models (LLMs). Yet, existing approaches often rely on heavyweight fine-tuning that is costly to update, audit, and maintain across model families. Full fine-tuning incurs substantial computational and storage overhead, while parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA trade efficiency for inconsistent safety gains and sensitivity to design choices. Safety intervention mechanisms such as circuit breakers reduce unsafe outputs without modifying model weights, but do not directly shape or preserve the internal representations that govern safety behavior. These limitations hinder rapid and reliable safety updates, particularly in settings where models evolve frequently or must adapt to new policies and domains. We present NeST, a lightweight, structure-aware safety alignment framework that strengthens refusal behavior by selectively adapting a small subset of safety-relevant neurons while freezing the remainder of the model. NeST aligns parameter updates with the internal organization of safety behavior by clustering functionally coherent safety neurons and enforcing shared updates within each cluster, enabling targeted and stable safety adaptation without broad model modification or inference-time overhead. We benchmark NeST against three dominant baselines: full fine-tuning, LoRA-based fine-tuning, and circuit breakers across 10 open-weight LLMs spanning multiple model families and sizes. Across all evaluated models, NeST reduces the attack success rate from an average of 44.5% to 4.36%, corresponding to a 90.2% reduction in unsafe generations, while requiring only 0.44 million trainable parameters on average. This amounts to a 17,310x decrease in updated parameters compared to full fine-tuning and a 9.25x reduction relative to LoRA, while consistently achieving stronger safety performance for alignment.

papers.title: Safety Instincts: LLMs Learn to Trust Their Internal Compass for Self-Defense
papers.research_question: Can models learn to enhance their own safety without relying on external validators by leveraging their internal confidence (entropy) signals?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that aligned models have an entropy gap between safe and unsafe responses and introduces SIRL, which uses this entropy as an intrinsic reward signal for self-alignment without external supervision.
papers.conclusion: Effective safety alignment can emerge from models' own confidence signals, paving the way for autonomous AI safety mechanisms that scale without extensive human oversight.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned models exhibit lower entropy (higher confidence) when generating safe refusals compared to harmful content.
SIRL achieves high defense success rates (over 89%) against diverse jailbreak attacks.
SIRL preserves or improves general capabilities (mathematics, coding, conversation) while enhancing safety.
SIRL is data-efficient, requiring only 15,000 unlabeled prompts.
SIRL generalizes to novel jailbreak techniques.
papers.abstract: Ensuring Large Language Model (LLM) safety remains challenging due to the absence of universal standards and reliable content validators, making it difficult to obtain effective training signals. We discover that aligned models already possess robust internal safety beliefs: they consistently produce high-confidence refusals to harmful requests while exhibiting high entropy when generating potentially dangerous content. This entropy gap reveals an untapped signal--models intrinsically "know" when to refuse. We introduce Safety Instincts Reinforcement Learning (SIRL), which transforms this internal confidence into a self-generated reward signal, eliminating dependence on external validators or human annotations. SIRL teaches models to trust their safety instincts by reinforcing low-entropy refusal behaviors. Evaluated on Llama and Qwen models, SIRL maintains 89%+ Defense Success Rates (DSRs) against 20+ jailbreak methods, from static prompts to adaptive attacks. Using only 15,000 unlabeled prompts, SIRL surpasses resource-intensive supervised methods while preserving performance on mathematics, coding, and conversation benchmarks. Our work demonstrates that effective alignment can emerge from within, paving the way for more autonomous and robust AI safety mechanisms that scale without extensive human oversight.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: Large Language Model Safety: A Holistic Survey
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the current landscape of LLM safety, covering four major risk categories (value misalignment, robustness to attack, misuse, autonomous AI risks) and related areas such as interpretability, technology roadmaps, and governance.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes that a holistic approach to LLM safety is necessary, integrating technical, ethical, and governance measures, and identifies future research directions.
papers.key_findings:
The survey categorizes LLM safety risks into four main areas: value misalignment, robustness to attack, misuse, and autonomous AI risks.
It highlights the importance of interpretability for enhancing LLM safety and the role of governance and international cooperation.
It emphasizes the necessity for a proactive, multifaceted approach integrating technical solutions, ethical considerations, and robust governance frameworks.
It identifies challenges and future directions, including exploring safe architectures, safety control modules, unified safety mechanisms, improved evaluations, and international cooperation.
future_direction: Exploring safe architectures for LLMs.
Developing safety control modules.
Improving safety evaluations for LLMs.
papers.abstract: The rapid development and deployment of large language models (LLMs) have introduced a new frontier in artificial intelligence, marked by unprecedented capabilities in natural language understanding and generation. However, the increasing integration of these models into critical applications raises substantial safety concerns, necessitating a thorough examination of their potential risks and associated mitigation strategies. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the current landscape of LLM safety, covering four major categories: value misalignment, robustness to adversarial attacks, misuse, and autonomous AI risks. In addition to the comprehensive review of the mitigation methodologies and evaluation resources on these four aspects, we further explore four topics related to LLM safety: the safety implications of LLM agents, the role of interpretability in enhancing LLM safety, the technology roadmaps proposed and abided by a list of AI companies and institutes for LLM safety, and AI governance aimed at LLM safety with discussions on international cooperation, policy proposals, and prospective regulatory directions. Our findings underscore the necessity for a proactive, multifaceted approach to LLM safety, emphasizing the integration of technical solutions, ethical considerations, and robust governance frameworks. This survey is intended to serve as a foundational resource for academy researchers, industry practitioners, and policymakers, offering insights into the challenges and opportunities associated with the safe integration of LLMs into society. Ultimately, it seeks to contribute to the safe and beneficial development of LLMs, aligning with the overarching goal of harnessing AI for societal advancement and well-being. A curated list of related papers has been publicly available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/Awesome-LLM-Safety-Papers.

papers.title: NeuRel-Attack: Neuron Relearning for Safety Disalignment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can safety alignment in large language models be bypassed by identifying and modifying specific neurons responsible for safety constraints?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NeuRel-Attack, a method to identify and modify neurons responsible for safety alignment in LLMs, enabling effective disalignment with minimal fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: NeuRel-Attack effectively removes safety constraints in LLMs by targeting specific neurons, demonstrating a critical vulnerability and the need for improved defensive strategies.
papers.key_findings:
NeuRel-Attack achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 96%, outperforming existing jailbreak methods.
The method reduces trainable parameters by up to 83% compared to standard LoRA fine-tuning.
Optimal neuron similarity threshold for attack success is 0.85, balancing neuron selection and editing precision.
MemFlex-based selective fine-tuning strategy is the most effective among tested optimization methods.
The approach highlights vulnerabilities in current alignment techniques, emphasizing the need for robust defenses.
papers.limitation:
Fine-tuning modifications may be detectable through forensic analysis.
The method is computationally intensive and may not scale well to larger models.
Raises ethical risks by potentially enabling misuse to circumvent safety measures.
Assumes safety alignment is localized to specific neurons, which may not always be the case.
future_direction: Developing effective defenses against fine-tuning jailbreaks to improve LLM safety.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) is achieved through fine-tuning mechanisms that regulate neuron activations to suppress harmful content. In this work, we propose a novel approach to induce disalignment by identifying and modifying the neurons responsible for safety constraints. Our method consists of three key steps: Neuron Activation Analysis, where we examine activation patterns in response to harmful and harmless prompts to detect neurons that are critical for distinguishing between harmful and harmless inputs; Similarity-Based Neuron Identification, which systematically locates the neurons responsible for safe alignment; and Neuron Relearning for Safety Removal, where we fine-tune these selected neurons to restore the model's ability to generate previously restricted responses. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively removes safety constraints with minimal fine-tuning, highlighting a critical vulnerability in current alignment techniques. Our findings underscore the need for robust defenses against adversarial fine-tuning attacks on LLMs.

papers.title: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models with applications to the financial services industry
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to understand the inner workings of large language models for financial services applications, specifically for compliance monitoring?
papers.core_contribution: This paper pioneers the application of mechanistic interpretability to financial services, designing algorithmic tasks for compliance monitoring and analyzing GPT-2 Small's attention patterns for identifying potential Fair Lending violations.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability techniques can be successfully applied to understand LLM behavior in financial compliance tasks, providing insights into the roles of specific attention heads and MLP layers.
papers.key_findings:
Heads 11.4, 8.9, and 6.3 contribute positively to the Fair Lending task completion, while heads 0.6, 11.0, and 10.7 contribute negatively.
MLP layers 2 and 4 significantly improve task completion, while MLP layer 10 and attention layer 0 decrease performance.
Activation patching reveals that heads 10.2, 10.7, and 11.3 (positive) and heads 9.6 and 10.6 (negative) play significant roles, with head 10.2's value vector being particularly important.
The Fair Lending compliance task is more complex than the IOI task, involving information processing across many layers rather than being localized to a few final layers.
Value patching has a more significant effect than key or query patching for important heads in later layers (9-11).
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to GPT-2 Small, a relatively small model, and may not generalize to larger, more powerful LLMs.
The financial compliance task is more complex than the IOI task, making circuit discovery more challenging and less localized.
future_direction: Conducting experiments with more powerful open-source LLMs such as Mistral 7B and Llama-2 7B.
Working on more algorithmic examples of compliance tasks in financial services and finding prompts that result in large logit differences.
Performing path patching as a more sophisticated circuit discovery approach for end-to-end circuit identification.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models exhibit remarkable capabilities across a broad spectrum of applications. Nevertheless, due to their intrinsic complexity, these models present substantial challenges in interpreting their internal decision-making processes. This lack of transparency poses critical challenges when it comes to their adaptation by financial institutions, where concerns and accountability regarding bias, fairness, and reliability are of paramount importance. Mechanistic interpretability aims at reverse engineering complex AI models such as transformers. In this paper, we are pioneering the use of mechanistic interpretability to shed some light on the inner workings of large language models for use in financial services applications. We offer several examples of how algorithmic tasks can be designed for compliance monitoring purposes. In particular, we investigate GPT-2 Small’s attention pattern when prompted to identify potential violation of Fair Lending laws. Using direct logit attribution, we study the contributions of each layer and its corresponding attention heads to the logit difference in the residual stream. Finally, we design clean and corrupted prompts and use activation patching as a causal intervention method to localize our task completion components further. We observe that the (positive) heads 10.2 (head 2, layer 10), 10.7, and 11.3, as well as the (negative) heads 9.6 and 10.6 play a significant role in the task completion.

papers.title: Analyzing And Editing Inner Mechanisms Of Backdoored Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms of backdoored language models and how do they process trigger inputs, such as switching to toxic language?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PCP ablation, a method to analyze and edit backdoor mechanisms in language models, and identifies early-layer MLP modules as crucial for the backdoor mechanism in combination with the initial embedding projection.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that PCP ablation is an effective tool for understanding and editing backdoor mechanisms in language models, and that constraining specific modules during fine-tuning can enhance model robustness against backdoor attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Early-layer MLP modules are most important for the backdoor mechanism in transformer-based language models, in combination with the initial embedding projection.
PCP ablation can be used to remove, insert, and modify backdoor mechanisms by replacing transformer modules with low-rank matrices based on principal components of their activations.
The backdoor robustness of large language models can be improved by locally constraining individual modules (e.g., freezing weights) during fine-tuning on potentially poisonous datasets.
In toy models, the backdoor mechanism can be successfully replicated and edited using low-rank PCP ablations of MLP modules.
In large models, PCP ablation can partially reinsert or weaken the backdoor mechanism, though with limitations due to the simplicity of the linear replacement.
papers.limitation: The introduced PCP ablation technique only corrects the ASR tendency and leads to an increase in validation loss, due to the simplicity and linearity of the replacement.
papers.abstract: Poisoning of data sets is a potential security threat to large language models that can lead to backdoored models. A description of the internal mechanisms of backdoored language models and how they process trigger inputs, e.g., when switching to toxic language, has yet to be found. In this work, we study the internal representations of transformer-based backdoored language models and determine early-layer MLP modules as most important for the backdoor mechanism in combination with the initial embedding projection. We use this knowledge to remove, insert, and modify backdoor mechanisms with engineered replacements that reduce the MLP module outputs to essentials for the backdoor mechanism. To this end, we introduce PCP ablation, where we replace transformer modules with low-rank matrices based on the principal components of their activations. We demonstrate our results on backdoored toy, backdoored large, and non-backdoored open-source models. We show that we can improve the backdoor robustness of large language models by locally constraining individual modules during fine-tuning on potentially poisonous data sets. Trigger warning: Offensive language.

papers.title: No Two Devils Alike: Unveiling Distinct Mechanisms of Fine-tuning Attacks
papers.research_question: While different fine-tuning attacks can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that two representative fine-tuning attacks (Explicit Harmful Attack and Identity-Shifting Attack) have distinct mechanisms for compromising an LLM's safety alignment, indicating the need for diverse defense strategies.
papers.conclusion: Different fine-tuning attacks exploit distinct mechanisms to compromise LLM safety, underscoring the need for varied and robust defense strategies.
papers.key_findings:
EHA aggressively disrupts the harmful instruction recognition stage by suppressing the transmission of harmful signals in upper layers, while ISA does not significantly impact this stage.
Both EHA and ISA disrupt the initial refusal tone generation, but EHA suppresses refusal tokens via MLPs in mid-layers, whereas ISA does not.
Both attacks impair the refusal response completion stage, with ISA having a greater impact, causing the model to persistently generate harmful content even with refusal prefixes.
Adding a safety-oriented system prompt only partially mitigates the impairment caused by the attacks.
The attacks cause representation shifts: EHA shifts representations more for harmful inputs, while ISA causes a shift orthogonal to the harmfulness direction.
papers.limitation:
The study only investigates two fine-tuning attacks (EHA and ISA), which do not encompass the full spectrum of possible attacks.
The analysis is conducted solely on Llama-2-7b-chat, limiting the generalizability of the findings to other models.
The investigation does not involve the mechanics of particular components (e.g., individual attention heads) due to scope constraints.
future_direction: Using trained probes at mid-layers to robustly detect harmful inputs without an external detector.
Developing more attack-resisting model manipulation methods for safeguarding, as current steering methods may be less effective on attacked models.
papers.abstract: The existing safety alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is found fragile and could be easily attacked through different strategies, such as through fine-tuning on a few harmful examples or manipulating the prefix of the generation results. However, the attack mechanisms of these strategies are still underexplored. In this paper, we ask the following question: \textit{while these approaches can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?} To answer this question, we break down the safeguarding process of an LLM when encountered with harmful instructions into three stages: (1) recognizing harmful instructions, (2) generating an initial refusing tone, and (3) completing the refusal response. Accordingly, we investigate whether and how different attack strategies could influence each stage of this safeguarding process. We utilize techniques such as logit lens and activation patching to identify model components that drive specific behavior, and we apply cross-model probing to examine representation shifts after an attack. In particular, we analyze the two most representative types of attack approaches: Explicit Harmful Attack (EHA) and Identity-Shifting Attack (ISA). Surprisingly, we find that their attack mechanisms diverge dramatically. Unlike ISA, EHA tends to aggressively target the harmful recognition stage. While both EHA and ISA disrupt the latter two stages, the extent and mechanisms of their attacks differ significantly. Our findings underscore the importance of understanding LLMs' internal safeguarding process and suggest that diverse defense mechanisms are required to effectively cope with various types of attacks.

papers.title: GSAE: Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders for Robust LLM Safety Steering
papers.research_question: How to effectively steer LLMs for safety by capturing distributed safety representations using graph-regularized sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAE) to capture distributed safety representations in LLMs, enabling effective runtime safety steering with high refusal rates and preserved utility.
papers.conclusion: GSAE provides a robust method for safety steering by learning distributed safety representations, achieving high safety discrimination and utility preservation across diverse models and attacks.
papers.key_findings:
GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%).
It maintains strong task accuracy on QA benchmarks (e.g., 70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K).
GSAE generalizes across multiple LLM families (LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, Phi) and scales.
It is robust against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining ≥90% refusal of harmful content.
Ablation studies show that graph regularization is essential for performance, and the dual-gating mechanism enables adaptive steering.
papers.limitation: The runtime steering mechanism incurs inference latency overhead, which can interfere with optimized serving engines.
future_direction: Decomposing distributed features into interpretable safety sub-categories.
Ensuring the robustness of the neuron co-activation graph to dataset biases and adversarial inputs.
Extending graph-regularized learning to multi-modal domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face critical safety challenges, as they can be manipulated to generate harmful content through adversarial prompts and jailbreak attacks. Many defenses are typically either black-box guardrails that filter outputs, or internals-based methods that steer hidden activations by operationalizing safety as a single latent feature or dimension. While effective for simple concepts, this assumption is limiting, as recent evidence shows that abstract concepts such as refusal and temporality are distributed across multiple features rather than isolated in one. To address this limitation, we introduce Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAEs), which extends SAEs with a Laplacian smoothness penalty on the neuron co-activation graph. Unlike standard SAEs that assign each concept to a single latent feature, GSAEs recover smooth, distributed safety representations as coherent patterns spanning multiple features. We empirically demonstrate that GSAE enables effective runtime safety steering, assembling features into a weighted set of safety-relevant directions and controlling them with a two-stage gating mechanism that activates interventions only when harmful prompts or continuations are detected during generation. This approach enforces refusals adaptively while preserving utility on benign queries. Across safety and QA benchmarks, GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%), while maintaining strong task accuracy (70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K). Robustness experiments further show generalization across LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, and Phi families and resilience against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining >= 90% refusal of harmful content.

papers.title: Do Internal Layers of LLMs Reveal Patterns for Jailbreak Detection?
papers.research_question: Do internal layers of LLMs reveal patterns for jailbreak detection? Specifically, how do hidden layers respond to jailbreak versus benign prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that analyzing internal layer representations of LLMs combined with tensor decomposition provides a promising approach for detecting jailbreak prompts.
papers.conclusion: Examining internal layer representations of LLMs combined with tensor decomposition techniques provides a promising approach for detecting jailbreak prompts, offering a simple, efficient, and effective pathway for improvement.
papers.key_findings:
For GPT-J, Multi-Head Attention (MHA) representations outperform layer outputs for jailbreak classification.
For Mamba-2, Mixer representations outperform Block outputs for jailbreak classification.
Tensor decomposition of internal representations yields latent factors that provide clear separation between jailbreak and benign prompts.
A simple pipeline of tensor decomposition followed by basic classifiers (e.g., Random Forest, SVM) achieves effective jailbreak detection.
papers.limitation: The study is preliminary and requires further work on larger datasets, additional architectures, and more sophisticated evaluation settings.
future_direction: Extend the methodology to larger datasets.
Apply the methodology to additional architectures.
Conduct more sophisticated evaluation.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a pressing concern with the increasing prevalence and accessibility of conversational LLMs. Adversarial users often exploit these models through carefully engineered prompts to elicit restricted or sensitive outputs, a strategy widely referred to as jailbreaking. While numerous defense mechanisms have been proposed, attackers continuously develop novel prompting techniques, and no existing model can be considered fully resistant. In this study, we investigate the jailbreak phenomenon by examining the internal representations of LLMs, with a focus on how hidden layers respond to jailbreak versus benign prompts. Specifically, we analyze the open-source LLM GPT-J and the state-space model Mamba2, presenting preliminary findings that highlight distinct layer-wise behaviors. Our results suggest promising directions for further research on leveraging internal model dynamics for robust jailbreak detection and defense.

papers.title: Internal Activation Revision: Safeguarding Vision Language Models Without Parameter Update
papers.research_question: Why are vision-language models (VLMs) more vulnerable to generating harmful content compared to their backbone large language models (LLMs), and how can they be safeguarded without parameter updates?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an internal activation revision framework that revises activations during generation to steer vision-language models toward safer outputs without updating model parameters.
papers.conclusion: The internal activation revision method effectively safeguards vision-language models by steering activations toward safer directions, demonstrating competitive results without parameter updates.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs are more vulnerable due to significant differences in internal activation distributions between text-only and image-text inputs, which safety alignments are not robust to handle.
The internal activation revision method significantly improves safety, reducing attack success rates by an average of 48.94%, 34.34%, 43.92%, and 52.98% on SafeBench, Safe-Unsafe, Unsafe, and MM-SafetyBench, respectively, with minimal impact on helpfulness.
Head-level revision achieves a better balance between safety and helpfulness than layer-level revision.
Multi-Response sample construction combined with mass mean shift (MMS) vector extraction yields the best performance.
Revision vectors extracted from one model show good transferability to other models with the same representation dimension.
papers.limitation: Sampling a portion of data from existing datasets may affect the accuracy of some conclusions.
papers.abstract: Warning: This paper contains offensive content that may disturb some readers. Vision-language models (VLMs) demonstrate strong multimodal capabilities but have been found to be more susceptible to generating harmful content compared to their backbone large language models (LLMs). Our investigation reveals that the integration of images significantly shifts the model's internal activations during the forward pass, diverging from those triggered by textual input. Moreover, the safety alignments of LLMs embedded within VLMs are not sufficiently robust to handle the activations discrepancies, making the models vulnerable to even the simplest jailbreaking attacks. To address this issue, we propose an internal activation revision approach that efficiently revises activations during generation, steering the model toward safer outputs. Our framework incorporates revisions at both the layer and head levels, offering control over the model's generation at varying levels of granularity. In addition, we explore three strategies for constructing positive and negative samples and two approaches for extracting revision vectors, resulting in different variants of our method. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that the internal activation revision method significantly improves the safety of widely used VLMs, reducing attack success rates by an average of 48.94%, 34.34%, 43.92%, and 52.98% on SafeBench, Safe-Unsafe, Unsafe, and MM-SafetyBench, respectively, while minimally impacting model helpfulness.

papers.title: Locking Down the Finetuned LLMs Safety
papers.research_question: How can we locate safety-relevant attention heads in a large scale of fine-tuned models and effectively obtain the safety vector for fine-tuned LLMs without negative transfer to other general tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafetyLock, a method to maintain safety in fine-tuned LLMs by extracting safety directions (Meta-SafetyLock) from the base model and applying them to fine-tuned models via activation intervention.
papers.conclusion: SafetyLock is an efficient method for maintaining the safety of fine-tuned LLMs, offering a scalable and effective approach to aligning models with ethical constraints while preserving utility.
papers.key_findings:
SafetyLock reduces the harmful instruction response rate from 60% to below 1% in toxic fine-tuned models.
SafetyLock can be applied in under 0.01 seconds without additional computational cost.
The safety-related activation patterns are largely preserved during fine-tuning, enabling transferable safety interventions.
SafetyLock maintains model performance on general tasks while significantly improving safety.
The method demonstrates robust defense against both fine-tuning vulnerabilities and prompt-based attacks.
future_direction: Explore SafetyLock's applicability to other model architectures.
Investigate its potential in multi-modal settings.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on additional datasets is often necessary to optimize them for specific downstream tasks. However, existing safety alignment measures, which restrict harmful behavior during inference, are insufficient to mitigate safety risks during fine-tuning. Alarmingly, fine-tuning with just 10 toxic sentences can make models comply with harmful instructions. We introduce SafetyLock, a novel alignment intervention method that maintains robust safety post-fine-tuning through efficient and transferable mechanisms. SafetyLock leverages our discovery that fine-tuned models retain similar safety-related activation representations to their base models. This insight enables us to extract what we term the Meta-SafetyLock, a set of safety bias directions representing key activation patterns associated with safe responses in the original model. We can then apply these directions universally to fine-tuned models to enhance their safety. By searching for activation directions across multiple token dimensions, SafetyLock achieves enhanced robustness and transferability. SafetyLock re-aligns fine-tuned models in under 0.01 seconds without additional computational cost. Our experiments demonstrate that SafetyLock can reduce the harmful instruction response rate from 60% to below 1% in toxic fine-tuned models. It surpasses traditional methods in both performance and efficiency, offering a scalable, non-invasive solution for ensuring the safety of customized LLMs. Our analysis across various fine-tuning scenarios confirms SafetyLock's robustness, advocating its integration into safety protocols for aligned LLMs. The code is released at https://github.com/zhu-minjun/SafetyLock.

papers.title: Representation Bending for Large Language Model Safety
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLM safety by bending the representation space to separate safe and unsafe representations, bringing activation steering to fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REPBEND, a method that brings activation steering to fine-tuning by bending the representation space to separate safe and unsafe representations, achieving state-of-the-art safety performance with minimal impact on general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: REPBEND effectively enhances LLM safety by bending representations to separate safe and unsafe states, achieving state-of-the-art performance with minimal impact on general capabilities, offering a scalable safety solution.
papers.key_findings:
REPBEND achieves up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks.
REPBEND maintains general capabilities and usability, with minimal degradation on standard benchmarks.
REPBEND outperforms prior methods such as Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO in both black-box and white-box attacks.
REPBEND works best when applied to mid-to-later layers of the transformer.
REPBEND's loss function, which includes L2 norm, cosine similarity, and KL divergence terms, effectively separates safe and unsafe representations.
papers.limitation:
REPBEND requires a dataset of safe and unsafe prompts, which may not cover all possible harmful scenarios.
The method relies on the choice of layers and hyperparameters, which may need tuning for different models.
The transferability of LoRA for safety improvements remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Exploring the transferability of LoRA adapters for safety across models.
Extending REPBEND to multimodal settings.
Investigating the theoretical foundations of representation bending.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools, but their inherent safety risks - ranging from harmful content generation to broader societal harms - pose significant challenges. These risks can be amplified by the recent adversarial attacks, fine-tuning vulnerabilities, and the increasing deployment of LLMs in high-stakes environments. Existing safety-enhancing techniques, such as fine-tuning with human feedback or adversarial training, are still vulnerable as they address specific threats and often fail to generalize across unseen attacks, or require manual system-level defenses. This paper introduces RepBend, a novel approach that fundamentally disrupts the representations underlying harmful behaviors in LLMs, offering a scalable solution to enhance (potentially inherent) safety. RepBend brings the idea of activation steering - simple vector arithmetic for steering model's behavior during inference - to loss-based fine-tuning. Through extensive evaluation, RepBend achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior methods such as Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO, with up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks, all with negligible reduction in model usability and general capabilities.

papers.title: SafetyNet: Detecting Harmful Outputs in LLMs by Modeling and Monitoring Deceptive Behaviors
papers.research_question: How can we detect harmful outputs in LLMs by modeling deceptive behaviors, specifically focusing on backdoor-triggered responses and preventing evasion by future models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Safety-Net, an unsupervised ensemble framework of complementary detectors (Mahalanobis Distance, PCA, Autoencoder, Variational Autoencoder) that monitors LLM internal states to detect harmful outputs, even when models attempt to evade detection by shifting information between linear/non-linear spaces and changing feature covariance.
papers.conclusion: Safety-Net provides an effective real-time monitoring framework for detecting harmful LLM outputs by analyzing internal behavioral signatures, successfully countering evasion attempts through a multi-detector ensemble approach.
papers.key_findings:
