Safety-Net, an ensemble of complementary detection monitors, effectively detects both straightforward harmful content in current models and disguised harmful content in deceptive future models.
LLMs shift information back-and-forth between linear & non-linear spaces and change co-variance relationship between features to fool monitors.
Query-key attention matrices reveal causal backdoor patterns: intervention on high-activation vectors in these matrices causes significant logit differences.
Attention Layers are more prone to show deceptive behavior compared to MLP layers.
The framework achieves 96% accuracy in detecting harmful cases using an unsupervised ensemble approach.
papers.abstract: High-risk industries like nuclear and aviation use real-time monitoring to detect dangerous system conditions. Similarly, Large Language Models (LLMs) need monitoring safeguards. We propose a real-time framework to predict harmful AI outputs before they occur by using an unsupervised approach that treats normal behavior as the baseline and harmful outputs as outliers. Our study focuses specifically on backdoor-triggered responses -- where specific input phrases activate hidden vulnerabilities causing the model to generate unsafe content like violence, pornography, or hate speech. We address two key challenges: (1) identifying true causal indicators rather than surface correlations, and (2) preventing advanced models from deception -- deliberately evading monitoring systems. Hence, we approach this problem from an unsupervised lens by drawing parallels to human deception: just as humans exhibit physical indicators while lying, we investigate whether LLMs display distinct internal behavioral signatures when generating harmful content. Our study addresses two critical challenges: 1) designing monitoring systems that capture true causal indicators rather than superficial correlations; and 2)preventing intentional evasion by increasingly capable "Future models''. Our findings show that models can produce harmful content through causal mechanisms and can become deceptive by: (a) alternating between linear and non-linear representations, and (b) modifying feature relationships. To counter this, we developed Safety-Net -- a multi-detector framework that monitors different representation dimensions, successfully detecting harmful behavior even when information is shifted across representational spaces to evade individual monitors. Our evaluation shows 96% accuracy in detecting harmful cases using our unsupervised ensemble approach.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: XAI for Transformers: Better Explanations through Conservative Propagation
papers.research_question: How to bring Explainable AI to Transformers in a theoretically sound manner, focusing on the axiom of conservation to reliably identify the contribution of input features to the prediction.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretically grounded extension of Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to Transformers by addressing conservation issues in attention heads and LayerNorm, leading to state-of-the-art explanation performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed LRP-based explanation method for Transformers addresses conservation issues and achieves state-of-the-art performance, contributing to safer and more transparent use of Transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient×Input fails to conserve relevance in Transformers due to attention heads and LayerNorm.
The proposed LRP rules (detaching gating and rescaling terms) restore conservation.
The proposed method outperforms existing explanation methods on a variety of Transformer models and datasets.
The method can be used to analyze bias in models without generating counterfactual examples.
papers.abstract: Transformers have become an important workhorse of machine learning, with numerous applications. This necessitates the development of reliable methods for increasing their transparency. Multiple interpretability methods, often based on gradient information, have been proposed. We show that the gradient in a Transformer reflects the function only locally, and thus fails to reliably identify the contribution of input features to the prediction. We identify Attention Heads and LayerNorm as main reasons for such unreliable explanations and propose a more stable way for propagation through these layers. Our proposal, which can be seen as a proper extension of the well-established LRP method to Transformers, is shown both theoretically and empirically to overcome the deficiency of a simple gradient-based approach, and achieves state-of-the-art explanation performance on a broad range of Transformer models and datasets.

papers.title: The Laminar Flow Hypothesis: Detecting Jailbreaks via Semantic Turbulence in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can jailbreaks in large language models be detected by analyzing the variance in layer-wise semantic trajectories?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Laminar Flow Hypothesis and Semantic Turbulence, a zero-shot metric for detecting jailbreaks in LLMs by analyzing internal latent trajectories, and demonstrates its ability to diagnose safety architectures.
papers.conclusion: Semantic Turbulence serves as an effective jailbreak detector and diagnostic tool for categorizing safety architectures in LLMs, based on the Laminar Flow Hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic Turbulence effectively discriminates between benign and adversarial inputs with statistical significance.
Qwen2-1.5B exhibits a 75.4% increase in turbulence under attack, indicating a conflict-based safety mechanism.
Gemma-2B shows a 22.0% decrease in turbulence, suggesting a reflex-based refusal mechanism.
Two distinct safety signatures are identified: conflict-based (high turbulence) and reflex-based (low turbulence).
The metric is lightweight, real-time, and requires no auxiliary training, making it suitable for deployment.
future_direction: scalability to larger models
robustness against adaptive attacks
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become ubiquitous, the challenge of securing them against adversarial "jailbreaking" attacks has intensified. Current defense strategies often rely on computationally expensive external classifiers or brittle lexical filters, overlooking the intrinsic dynamics of the model's reasoning process. In this work, the Laminar Flow Hypothesis is introduced, which posits that benign inputs induce smooth, gradual transitions in an LLM's high-dimensional latent space, whereas adversarial prompts trigger chaotic, high-variance trajectories - termed Semantic Turbulence - resulting from the internal conflict between safety alignment and instruction-following objectives. This phenomenon is formalized through a novel, zero-shot metric: the variance of layer-wise cosine velocity. Experimental evaluation across diverse small language models reveals a striking diagnostic capability. The RLHF-aligned Qwen2-1.5B exhibits a statistically significant 75.4% increase in turbulence under attack (p less than 0.001), validating the hypothesis of internal conflict. Conversely, Gemma-2B displays a 22.0% decrease in turbulence, characterizing a distinct, low-entropy "reflex-based" refusal mechanism. These findings demonstrate that Semantic Turbulence serves not only as a lightweight, real-time jailbreak detector but also as a non-invasive diagnostic tool for categorizing the underlying safety architecture of black-box models.

papers.title: DiffuGuard: How Intrinsic Safety is Lost and Found in Diffusion Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the unique safety vulnerabilities of Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) arising from their iterative and parallel generation mechanisms, and how can they be effectively defended against?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes two unique vulnerabilities in dLLMs (intra-step greedy remasking bias and inter-step denoising-path dependence) and proposes DIFFUGUARD, a training-free defense framework that uses stochastic annealing remasking and block-level audit and repair to significantly reduce jailbreak success rates while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that dLLMs have unique vulnerabilities due to their parallel and iterative generation, and proposes DIFFUGUARD, an effective training-free defense that significantly improves safety with minimal impact on performance.
papers.key_findings:
There exists a core Safety-Quality trade-off in dLLM decoding: introducing randomness can improve safety, but often at the cost of sacrificing generation quality.
The dLLM generation process is characterized by a strong Denoising-path Dependence, where the safety established in early steps has a decisive influence on the final output.
DIFFUGUARD reduces the average Attack Success Rate (ASR) against six diverse jailbreak methods from 47.9% to 14.7%.
DIFFUGUARD has minimal impact on model utility and efficiency, making it a practical plug-and-play defense.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation primarily uses jailbreak attack algorithms validated on AR LLMs, as dLLM-specific attack techniques are still emerging.
DIFFUGUARD is a training-free inference-time defense; for attacks deeply exploiting model mechanisms, safety alignment training is another important complementary path.
future_direction: Explore more dLLM-specific attack and defense techniques.
Integrate training-free defense strategies like DIFFUGUARD with model safety alignment training, e.g., using detected attack samples for adversarial training.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) introduces unprecedented vulnerabilities that are fundamentally distinct from Autoregressive LLMs, stemming from their iterative and parallel generation mechanisms. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of dLLM vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks across two distinct dimensions: intra-step and inter-step dynamics. Experimental results reveal a harmful bias inherent in the standard greedy remasking strategy and identify a critical phenomenon we term Denoising-path Dependence, where the safety of early-stage tokens decisively influences the final output. These findings also indicate that while current decoding strategies constitute a significant vulnerability, dLLMs possess a substantial intrinsic safety potential. To unlock this potential, we propose DiffuGuard, a training-free defense framework that addresses vulnerabilities through a dual-stage approach: Stochastic Annealing Remasking dynamically introduces controlled randomness to mitigate greedy selection bias, while Block-level Audit and Repair exploits internal model representations for autonomous risk detection and guided correction. Comprehensive experiments on four dLLMs demonstrate DiffuGuard's exceptional effectiveness, reducing Attack Success Rate against six diverse jailbreak methods from 47.9% to 14.7% while preserving model utility and efficiency. Our code is available at: https://github.com/niez233/DiffuGuard.

papers.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: How is arithmetic ability implemented in large language models, specifically the role of attention heads and FFN neurons, and what is the internal logic chain from input to prediction? Additionally, how does the LoRA fine-tuning method work?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method to interpret arithmetic mechanisms in LLMs, identifying an internal logic chain of four stages, and applies it to understand LoRA and for model pruning and bias reduction.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies important attention heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic, proposes the CNA method to construct the internal logic chain, finds LoRA amplifies important FFN neurons, and applies CNA to model pruning and editing.
papers.key_findings:
Arithmetic ability is localized in a few attention heads (arithmetic heads), each specializing in distinct operations.
The internal logic chain from input to prediction consists of four stages: feature enhancing, feature transferring, feature predicting, and prediction enhancing.
LoRA enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of important FFN neurons related to the final prediction.
Model pruning retaining only 5% of deep FFN neurons identified by CNA maintains performance on arithmetic tasks.
Model editing by zeroing 18 FFN neurons identified by CNA reduces gender bias by 35.7%.
papers.limitation:
The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vocabulary space, which is empirically interpretable but lacks complete theoretical foundation.
There is a lack of standardization across various studies regarding attribution methods (e.g., different intervention methods).
A potential risk is that attackers can identify and edit important neurons to change model behavior maliciously.
future_direction: Further investigation of the multiplication heads which do not significantly impact accuracy.
Explorations on different datasets for gender bias reduction.
Distinguishing whether a model has been edited to prevent malicious use.

papers.title: Monolingual and Multilingual Reduction of Gender Bias in Contextualized Representations
papers.research_question: How can we effectively reduce gender bias in contextualized representations using DensRay, and how is gender information distributed in BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using DensRay to debias contextualized representations, showing it performs comparably to prior methods, is more robust, preserves language model performance better, and enables multilingual debiasing.
papers.conclusion: DensRay is an effective method for reducing gender bias in contextualized representations, maintaining model performance, and can be applied multilingually.
papers.key_findings:
DensRay effectively mitigates gender bias on OCCTMP and association tests.
DensRay preserves language model performance on Wikitext-2 and GLUE tasks better than other methods.
Gender information is spread across all attention heads and most layers in BERT, with no single head responsible.
DensRay can obtain gender bias scores on token and sentence levels.
DensRay can be used for zero-shot multilingual debiasing (e.g., debias Chinese using English data).
papers.limitation:
Token-level bias scores work well for monolingual BERT but not for multilingual BERT.
The method focuses only on the gender direction and may not address biases from implicitly gendered terms.
future_direction: Investigate multilingual transfer of debiasing techniques more closely.
Investigate debiasing with non-binary approaches (beyond male-female binary).
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (PLMs) learn stereotypes held by humans and reflected in text from their training corpora, including gender bias. When PLMs are used for downstream tasks such as picking candidates for a job, people's lives can be negatively affected by these learned stereotypes. Prior work usually identifies a linear gender subspace and removes gender information by eliminating the subspace. Following this line of work, we propose to use DensRay, an analytical method for obtaining interpretable dense subspaces. We show that DensRay performs on-par with prior approaches, but provide arguments that it is more robust and provide indications that it preserves language model performance better. By applying DensRay to attention heads and layers of BERT we show that gender information is spread across all attention heads and most of the layers. Also we show that DensRay can obtain gender bias scores on both token and sentence levels. Finally, we demonstrate that we can remove bias multilingually, e.g., from Chinese, using only English training data.

papers.title: AdvJudge-Zero: Binary Decision Flips in LLM-as-a-Judge via Adversarial Control Tokens
papers.research_question: How can short sequences of low-perplexity control tokens flip binary evaluations in LLM-as-a-Judge systems, representing a reward-hacking risk in post-training pipelines?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AdvJudge-Zero, a zero-seed method to discover adversarial control tokens that flip binary decisions in LLM-as-a-Judge systems, and shows these tokens represent a realistic reward-hacking risk in post-training pipelines.
papers.conclusion: LLM-as-a-Judge systems are vulnerable to adversarial control tokens that flip binary decisions, and adversarial training can mitigate this risk.
papers.key_findings:
AdvJudge-Zero achieves very high false positive rates (up to 100%) on various models and datasets.
The adversarial tokens are low-perplexity and model-intrinsic, generalizing across models.
The vulnerability stems from a shallow, high-gain decision boundary at the last layer.
LoRA-based adversarial training can reduce false positives while preserving evaluation quality.
Specialized judge models exhibit varying robustness, with Omni-Judge being highly vulnerable and general-verifier being robust.
papers.limitation:
Focuses only on binary evaluations and false-positive flips, not on inducing harmful content or bypassing safety filters.
Does not release attack prompts or control-token sequences to prevent malicious use.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-turn dialogues and conversational judges.
Studying other judge architectures and training objectives.
Integrating adversarial training into post-training pipelines like RLHF and DPO.
papers.abstract: Reward models and LLM-as-a-Judge systems are central to modern post-training pipelines such as RLHF, DPO, and RLAIF, where they provide scalar feedback and binary decisions that guide model selection and RL-based fine-tuning. We show that these judge systems exhibit a recurring vulnerability: short sequences of low-perplexity control tokens can flip many binary evaluations from correct ``No'' judgments to incorrect ``Yes'' judgments by steering the last-layer logit gap. These control tokens are patterns that a policy model could plausibly generate during post-training, and thus represent realistic reward-hacking risks rather than worst-case adversarial strings. Our method, AdvJudge-Zero, uses the model's next-token distribution and beam-search exploration to discover diverse control-token sequences from scratch, and our analysis shows that the induced hidden-state perturbations concentrate in a low-rank ``soft mode'' that is anti-aligned with the judge's refusal direction. Empirically, these tokens cause very high false positive rates when large open-weight and specialized judge models score incorrect answers on math and reasoning benchmarks. Finally, we show that LoRA-based adversarial training on small sets of control-token-augmented examples can markedly reduce these false positives while preserving evaluation quality.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning can Distort Pretrained Features and Underperform Out-of-Distribution
papers.research_question: Under what conditions does fine-tuning underperform linear probing out-of-distribution, and how can this be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning can distort pretrained features and underperform linear probing out-of-distribution when pretrained features are good and distribution shift is large; linear probing then full fine-tuning (LP-FT) combines the benefits of both methods.
papers.conclusion: LP-FT is a simple, effective method for robust fine-tuning that mitigates the tradeoff between in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning achieves higher in-distribution accuracy but lower out-of-distribution accuracy than linear probing on large distribution shifts.
Theoretical analysis shows fine-tuning distorts pretrained features because the feature extractor changes more for in-distribution examples than out-of-distribution examples.
Linear probing preserves pretrained features and extrapolates better out-of-distribution but cannot adapt features to the downstream task.
LP-FT (linear probing then fine-tuning) outperforms both fine-tuning and linear probing in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy.
Feature distortion in fine-tuning is due to random head initialization; initializing with a linear probed head reduces distortion.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis is limited to linear models and may not capture all aspects of deep neural networks.
future_direction: Extend theoretical analysis to non-linear models and neural tangent kernel regime.
Develop even better methods for robust fine-tuning inspired by the analysis.
papers.abstract: When transferring a pretrained model to a downstream task, two popular methods are full fine-tuning (updating all the model parameters) and linear probing (updating only the last linear layer -- the "head"). It is well known that fine-tuning leads to better accuracy in-distribution (ID). However, in this paper, we find that fine-tuning can achieve worse accuracy than linear probing out-of-distribution (OOD) when the pretrained features are good and the distribution shift is large. On 10 distribution shift datasets (Breeds-Living17, Breeds-Entity30, DomainNet, CIFAR $\to$ STL, CIFAR10.1, FMoW, ImageNetV2, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, ImageNet-Sketch), fine-tuning obtains on average 2% higher accuracy ID but 7% lower accuracy OOD than linear probing. We show theoretically that this tradeoff between ID and OOD accuracy arises even in a simple setting: fine-tuning overparameterized two-layer linear networks. We prove that the OOD error of fine-tuning is high when we initialize with a fixed or random head -- this is because while fine-tuning learns the head, the lower layers of the neural network change simultaneously and distort the pretrained features. Our analysis suggests that the easy two-step strategy of linear probing then full fine-tuning (LP-FT), sometimes used as a fine-tuning heuristic, combines the benefits of both fine-tuning and linear probing. Empirically, LP-FT outperforms both fine-tuning and linear probing on the above datasets (1% better ID, 10% better OOD than full fine-tuning).

papers.title: OR-Bench: An Over-Refusal Benchmark for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure over-refusal in large language models, and what is the trade-off between safety and over-refusal?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OR-Bench, the first large-scale over-refusal benchmark, and uses it to evaluate 32 LLMs, revealing a strong correlation between safety and over-refusal.
papers.conclusion: OR-Bench provides a large-scale benchmark for evaluating over-refusal, facilitating future research on the trade-off between safety and helpfulness in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
There is a strong correlation between safety and over-refusal (Spearman rank correlation 0.89).
Claude models demonstrate the highest safety but also the most over-refusal.
Mistral models accept most prompts (low over-refusal).
GPT-3.5-turbo exhibits decreasing over-refusal in later versions, but with reduced safety.
Model size does not necessarily correlate with better safety-sensitivity balance.
papers.limitation:
The use of LLM as the moderator may result in the dataset including toxic or debatable prompts.
There may be bias favoring the LLMs used as judges.
future_direction: Future safety alignment algorithms should consider both toxic and over-refusal prompts to achieve improved safety alignment.
Further exploration of fine-tuning LLMs as judges for moderation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) require careful safety alignment to prevent malicious outputs. While significant research focuses on mitigating harmful content generation, the enhanced safety often come with the side effect of over-refusal, where LLMs may reject innocuous prompts and become less helpful. Although the issue of over-refusal has been empirically observed, a systematic measurement is challenging due to the difficulty of crafting prompts that can elicit the over-refusal behaviors of LLMs. This study proposes a novel method for automatically generating large-scale over-refusal datasets. Leveraging this technique, we introduce OR-Bench, the first large-scale over-refusal benchmark. OR-Bench comprises 80,000 over-refusal prompts across 10 common rejection categories, a subset of around 1,000 hard prompts that are challenging even for state-of-the-art LLMs, and an additional 600 toxic prompts to prevent indiscriminate responses. We then conduct a comprehensive study to measure the over-refusal of 32 popular LLMs across 8 model families. Our datasets are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/bench-llms and our codebase is open-sourced at https://github.com/justincui03/or-bench. We hope this benchmark can help the community develop better safety aligned models.

papers.title: MEUV: Achieving Fine-Grained Capability Activation in Large Language Models via Mutually Exclusive Unlock Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we achieve fine-grained capability activation in large language models to unlock specific hazardous topics while keeping others locked, as opposed to existing coarse methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MEUV, a lightweight framework that factorizes the monolithic refusal direction into topic-aligned, nearly orthogonal vectors, enabling fine-grained capability activation with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: MEUV demonstrates that the security layer of large language models can be selectively disabled with minimal impact on model utility, enabling controllable deployment in high-risk scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
MEUV achieves an attack success rate of at least 87% on Gemma-2-2B, LLaMA-3-8B, and Qwen-7B.
MEUV reduces cross-topic leakage by up to 90% compared to the best single-direction baseline.
Unlock vectors trained in one language transfer almost unchanged to another, suggesting a language-agnostic refusal subspace.
The framework is pluggable during inference and does not require modification of model weights.
The fine-grained decomposition of the refusal mechanism is achievable with minimal impact on model utility.
papers.limitation:
Relies on synthetic data and manual topic labels.
Theoretical guarantees assume a fixed router and do not cover adversarial prompt evolution.
future_direction: Extending the framework to open-vocabulary safety settings.
Exploring jointly robust routing strategies and automated topic discovery.
Applications to alignment-preserving reinforcement learning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) enforce safety alignment to reliably refuse malicious requests, yet the same blanket safeguards also block legitimate uses in policing, defense, and other high-stakes settings. Earlier "refusal-direction" edits can bypass those layers, but they rely on a single vector that indiscriminately unlocks all hazardous topics, offering no semantic control. We introduce Mutually Exclusive Unlock Vectors (MEUV), a lightweight framework that factorizes the monolithic refusal direction into topic-aligned, nearly orthogonal vectors, each dedicated to one sensitive capability. MEUV is learned in a single epoch with a multi-task objective that blends a differential-ablation margin, cross-topic and orthogonality penalties, and several auxiliary terms. On bilingual malicious-prompt benchmarks, MEUV achieves an attack success rate of no less than 87% on Gemma-2-2B, LLaMA-3-8B, and Qwen-7B, yet cuts cross-topic leakage by up to 90% compared with the best single-direction baseline. Vectors trained in Chinese transfer almost unchanged to English (and vice versa), suggesting a language-agnostic refusal subspace. The results show that fine-grained, topic-level capability activation is achievable with minimal utility loss, paving the way for controlled LLMs deployment in security-sensitive domains.

papers.title: Model Tampering Attacks Enable More Rigorous Evaluations of LLM Capabilities
papers.research_question: How vulnerable are LLMs to model tampering attacks (modifications to latent activations or weights), and can these attacks inform evaluators about LLM vulnerabilities to novel input-space attacks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces model tampering attacks as a complementary evaluation method for LLMs, showing that they can predict input-space vulnerabilities and that state-of-the-art unlearning methods are brittle to fine-tuning attacks.
papers.conclusion: Model tampering attacks enable substantially more rigorous evaluations of LLM capabilities and risks than input-space attacks alone, highlighting the difficulty of suppressing harmful capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Model tampering attacks are efficient and effective at eliciting harmful capabilities from LLMs.
Model robustness to a variety of capability elicitation attacks lies on a low-dimensional subspace.
The success rate of model tampering attacks correlates with and can conservatively estimate the success of held-out input-space attacks.
State-of-the-art unlearning methods can be reversed within a few steps of fine-tuning (sometimes as few as one step).
Representation rerouting (RR) achieved the highest unlearning score, but no unlearning method was robust to all attacks.
papers.limitation: Model tampering attack success on one task (WMDP-Bio) was not strongly predictive of model performance on a different task (UK AISI bio evaluation), suggesting a limitation in generalizing across task distributions.
papers.abstract: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) risks and capabilities are increasingly being incorporated into AI risk management and governance frameworks. Currently, most risk evaluations are conducted by designing inputs that elicit harmful behaviors from the system. However, this approach suffers from two limitations. First, input-output evaluations cannot fully evaluate realistic risks from open-weight models. Second, the behaviors identified during any particular input-output evaluation can only lower-bound the model's worst-possible-case input-output behavior. As a complementary method for eliciting harmful behaviors, we propose evaluating LLMs with model tampering attacks which allow for modifications to latent activations or weights. We pit state-of-the-art techniques for removing harmful LLM capabilities against a suite of 5 input-space and 6 model tampering attacks. In addition to benchmarking these methods against each other, we show that (1) model resilience to capability elicitation attacks lies on a low-dimensional robustness subspace; (2) the success rate of model tampering attacks can empirically predict and offer conservative estimates for the success of held-out input-space attacks; and (3) state-of-the-art unlearning methods can easily be undone within 16 steps of fine-tuning. Together, these results highlight the difficulty of suppressing harmful LLM capabilities and show that model tampering attacks enable substantially more rigorous evaluations than input-space attacks alone.

papers.title: Attributing Fair Decisions with Attention Interventions
papers.research_question: How can attention weights be used to attribute fairness and accuracy of a model, and how can bias be mitigated by manipulating attention weights?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an attention-based attribution framework that can identify features responsible for model fairness and accuracy, and proposes a post-processing bias mitigation strategy by manipulating attention weights.
papers.conclusion: The attention-based attribution framework is effective for fairness attribution and bias mitigation, providing interpretability and flexibility across tabular and text data.
papers.key_findings:
The attribution framework correctly identifies features responsible for accuracy and fairness in synthetic data.
The framework captures indirect discrimination where proxy features contribute more to unfairness than the sensitive attribute.
The post-processing mitigation strategy by reducing attention weights of unfair features is competitive with state-of-the-art methods.
The method is effective on both tabular and text data, reducing bias in occupation classification.
The method provides interpretability by showing which features are used for predictions.
papers.limitation:
The framework may be used for fairwashing (generating fake explanations for unfair decisions).
The framework is vulnerable to adversarial attacks.
The method does not achieve the best accuracy-fairness trade-off on the UCI Adult dataset for statistical parity.
future_direction: Improving the fairness-accuracy trade-off by considering the trade-off each feature contributes to both accuracy and fairness.
papers.abstract: The widespread use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in consequential domains, such as healthcare and parole decision-making systems, has drawn intense scrutiny on the fairness of these methods. However, ensuring fairness is often insufficient as the rationale for a contentious decision needs to be audited, understood, and defended. We propose that the attention mechanism can be used to ensure fair outcomes while simultaneously providing feature attributions to account for how a decision was made. Toward this goal, we design an attention-based model that can be leveraged as an attribution framework. It can identify features responsible for both performance and fairness of the model through attention interventions and attention weight manipulation. Using this attribution framework, we then design a post-processing bias mitigation strategy and compare it with a suite of baselines. We demonstrate the versatility of our approach by conducting experiments on two distinct data types, tabular and textual.

papers.title: Jailbreak Instruction-Tuned LLMs via end-of-sentence MLP Re-weighting
papers.research_question: How does re-weighting MLP neurons in end-of-sentence inferences affect the safety mechanisms of instruction-tuned LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences are critical for safety in instruction-tuned LLMs, and introduces two white-box jailbreak methods that re-weight MLP neurons to compromise safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences are critical for safety in instruction-tuned LLMs, and that re-weighting these neurons can effectively jailbreak the models, providing insights for both attack and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Re-weighting MLP neurons in end-of-sentence inferences can significantly compromise the safety of instruction-tuned LLMs.
The prompt-specific jailbreak method outperforms state-of-the-art prompt-specific methods and requires less computational time.
The prompt-general jailbreak method is comparable to state-of-the-art approaches and has minimal impact on the model's original capabilities (except for very small models).
The safety mechanism of instruction-tuned LLMs heavily relies on MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences.
The method can also serve as a mechanism interpretability tool to identify MLP neurons strongly correlated with safety.
papers.limitation:
The method is heuristic-driven, making it more of a validation experiment rather than an optimal solution.
The precise role MLP layers play in the safety mechanism and how they impact subsequent generation processes remain open questions.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the safety mechanisms of instruction fine-tuned large language models (LLMs). We discover that re-weighting MLP neurons can significantly compromise a model's safety, especially for MLPs in end-of-sentence inferences. We hypothesize that LLMs evaluate the harmfulness of prompts during end-of-sentence inferences, and MLP layers plays a critical role in this process. Based on this hypothesis, we develop 2 novel white-box jailbreak methods: a prompt-specific method and a prompt-general method. The prompt-specific method targets individual prompts and optimizes the attack on the fly, while the prompt-general method is pre-trained offline and can generalize to unseen harmful prompts. Our methods demonstrate robust performance across 7 popular open-source LLMs, size ranging from 2B to 72B. Furthermore, our study provides insights into vulnerabilities of instruction-tuned LLM's safety and deepens the understanding of the internal mechanisms of LLMs.

papers.title: Jailbreaking Leaves a Trace: Understanding and Detecting Jailbreak Attacks from Internal Representations of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal representations of LLMs differ between jailbreak and benign prompts, and can these differences be used for detection and mitigation?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak prompts leave identifiable traces in internal representations; a tensor-based framework can detect and mitigate jailbreaks by bypassing susceptible layers without model fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations contain strong and consistent signals for jailbreak detection and mitigation, providing a lightweight, architecture-agnostic direction for improving LLM security.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak and benign prompts exhibit distinct layer-dependent latent signatures in internal representations.
These signatures can be uncovered using tensor decomposition and used for detection with high F1 scores.
Layer-wise susceptibility scores can identify layers that strongly encode jailbreak features.
Bypassing susceptible layers at inference time can block 78% of jailbreak attempts while preserving 94% of benign prompts.
The patterns are consistent across diverse model families (transformer and state-space models).
papers.limitation: Persona- or roleplay-based prompt injections can persist even after bypassing susceptible layers, and the fixed probability threshold for bypassing may not capture attacks that distribute influence across multiple layers.
future_direction: Extending the framework to additional attack families (e.g., GCG, PAIR) by incorporating corresponding prompt distributions during factor learning.
Adopting adaptive or cumulative susceptibility criteria for layer bypass.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a critical security challenge with the widespread deployment of conversational AI systems. Adversarial users exploit these models through carefully crafted prompts to elicit restricted or unsafe outputs, a phenomenon commonly referred to as Jailbreaking. Despite numerous proposed defense mechanisms, attackers continue to develop adaptive prompting strategies, and existing models remain vulnerable. This motivates approaches that examine the internal behavior of LLMs rather than relying solely on prompt-level defenses. In this work, we study jailbreaking from both security and interpretability perspectives by analyzing how internal representations differ between jailbreak and benign prompts. We conduct a systematic layer-wise analysis across multiple open-source models, including GPT-J, LLaMA, Mistral, and the state-space model Mamba, and identify consistent latent-space patterns associated with harmful inputs. We then propose a tensor-based latent representation framework that captures structure in hidden activations and enables lightweight jailbreak detection without model fine-tuning or auxiliary LLM-based detectors. We further demonstrate that the latent signals can be used to actively disrupt jailbreak execution at inference time. On an abliterated LLaMA-3.1-8B model, selectively bypassing high-susceptibility layers blocks 78% of jailbreak attempts while preserving benign behavior on 94% of benign prompts. This intervention operates entirely at inference time and introduces minimal overhead, providing a scalable foundation for achieving stronger coverage by incorporating additional attack distributions or more refined susceptibility thresholds. Our results provide evidence that jailbreak behavior is rooted in identifiable internal structures and suggest a complementary, architecture-agnostic direction for improving LLM security.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Defending Large Language Models Against Attacks With Residual Stream Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: How can residual stream activations in LLMs be used to detect and classify adversarial attack prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a defense method that uses residual stream activations and a LightGBM classifier to detect adversarial attack prompts with high accuracy across multiple LLMs and attack scenarios.
papers.conclusion: The classification method using residual activations is promising for detecting attack prompts, but does not generalize to unseen attacks and is most useful when prompt classes are not easily distinguishable.
papers.key_findings:
The classifier achieves high accuracy (over 99%) for broad, domain-specific, and hyper-specific attack datasets across multiple LLMs.
The classifier does not rely on prompt length as a proxy for class, as shown by length restriction experiments.
The classifier fails to generalize to unseen attack types (holdout test).
The classifier performs less well on the WildJailBreak dataset where prompt classes are similar.
Fine-tuning with LoRA does not significantly improve classification accuracy.
papers.limitation: The methodology does not generalize to unseen attack types (attacks not in the training set).
future_direction: Explore more fine-tuning strategies to improve classification accuracy.
papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs), exemplified by OpenAI's ChatGPT, brings to the forefront the imperative to defend against adversarial threats on these models. These attacks, which manipulate an LLM's output by introducing malicious inputs, undermine the model's integrity and the trust users place in its outputs. In response to this challenge, our paper presents an innovative defensive strategy, given white box access to an LLM, that harnesses residual activation analysis between transformer layers of the LLM. We apply a novel methodology for analyzing distinctive activation patterns in the residual streams for attack prompt classification. We curate multiple datasets to demonstrate how this method of classification has high accuracy across multiple types of attack scenarios, including our newly-created attack dataset. Furthermore, we enhance the model's resilience by integrating safety fine-tuning techniques for LLMs in order to measure its effect on our capability to detect attacks. The results underscore the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing the detection and mitigation of adversarial inputs, advancing the security framework within which LLMs operate.

papers.title: Steering Externalities: Benign Activation Steering Unintentionally Increases Jailbreak Risk for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do steering vectors learned from benign instruction data have unintended side-effects on model safety? Specifically, does benign activation steering (for utility) unintentionally increase jailbreak risk for LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies 'steering externalities', a phenomenon where benign activation steering (e.g., for compliance or JSON formatting) unintentionally erodes safety guardrails and significantly increases jailbreak vulnerability in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering for utility creates steering externalities that increase jailbreak risk; steered deployments should be red-teamed, and future work should develop safety-aware steering to preserve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Benign activation steering (STEER-COMPLIANCE, STEER-JSON) increases Attack Success Rates (ASR) for jailbreak attacks, acting as a 'force multiplier' that can boost ASR to over 80-99% on standard benchmarks.
Steering shifts the internal representations of harmful prompts towards regions associated with harmless requests, reducing the model's 'safety margin' and making refusal less likely.
The safety degradation occurs because steering biases the early-token distribution away from refusal prefixes, making the model more likely to enter a non-refusal generation trajectory.
The effect is observed across multiple models (Llama-2, Llama-3, Gemma) and is amplified by existing black-box jailbreak methods like CoP, PAIR, and TAP.
A preliminary safety-aware steering method (STEER-BIND) can partially mitigate the externality, suggesting a path for future safer steering techniques.
papers.limitation: t-SNE visualizations are qualitative projections and the 2D boundary is only an illustrative diagnostic.
future_direction: Develop safety-aware steering vectors (like STEER-BIND) that preserve robustness.
Include broader alignment evaluations (beyond safety refusal) when auditing steered models.
Routine red-teaming and regression testing of steered model configurations before deployment.
papers.abstract: Activation steering is a practical post-training model alignment technique to enhance the utility of Large Language Models (LLMs). Prior to deploying a model as a service, developers can steer a pre-trained model toward specific behavioral objectives, such as compliance or instruction adherence, without the need for retraining. This process is as simple as adding a steering vector to the model's internal representations. However, this capability unintentionally introduces critical and under-explored safety risks. We identify a phenomenon termed Steering Externalities, where steering vectors derived from entirely benign datasets-such as those enforcing strict compliance or specific output formats like JSON-inadvertently erode safety guardrails. Experiments reveal that these interventions act as a force multiplier, creating new vulnerabilities to jailbreaks and increasing attack success rates to over 80% on standard benchmarks by bypassing the initial safety alignment. Ultimately, our results expose a critical blind spot in deployment: benign activation steering systematically erodes the "safety margin," rendering models more vulnerable to black-box attacks and proving that inference-time utility improvements must be rigorously audited for unintended safety externalities.

papers.title: Uncovering Safety Risks of Large Language Models through Concept Activation Vector
papers.research_question: How can safety risks of large language models be uncovered by interpreting their safety mechanisms and generating effective attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Safety Concept Activation Vector framework to interpret LLM safety mechanisms and develops an SCAV-guided attack method that generates effective attacks with automatic hyperparameter selection, improving attack success rates and response quality.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers severe safety risks in current LLMs and provides insights into their safety mechanisms using the SCAV framework.
papers.key_findings:
SCAV significantly improves attack success rates and response quality compared to baselines.
Generated attacks are transferable to black-box models like GPT-4 and other white-box LLMs.
Aligned LLMs show high vulnerability with average attack success rates up to 99.14%.
Existing unlearn methods may not fully erase harmful knowledge, as attacks still succeed.
Linear separability of embeddings indicates the formation of safety mechanisms in LLMs.
future_direction: Extending SCAV to multimodal models
Developing more robust defense methods against attacks
papers.abstract: Despite careful safety alignment, current large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to various attacks. To further unveil the safety risks of LLMs, we introduce a Safety Concept Activation Vector (SCAV) framework, which effectively guides the attacks by accurately interpreting LLMs' safety mechanisms. We then develop an SCAV-guided attack method that can generate both attack prompts and embedding-level attacks with automatically selected perturbation hyperparameters. Both automatic and human evaluations demonstrate that our attack method significantly improves the attack success rate and response quality while requiring less training data. Additionally, we find that our generated attack prompts may be transferable to GPT-4, and the embedding-level attacks may also be transferred to other white-box LLMs whose parameters are known. Our experiments further uncover the safety risks present in current LLMs. For example, in our evaluation of seven open-source LLMs, we observe an average attack success rate of 99.14%, based on the classic keyword-matching criterion. Finally, we provide insights into the safety mechanism of LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/SproutNan/AI-Safety_SCAV.

papers.title: Triggers Hijack Language Circuits: A Mechanistic Analysis of Backdoor Behaviors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do backdoor triggers operate inside the model? Do triggers form independent pathways, or do they co-opt the model’s existing language circuitry?
papers.core_contribution: Backdoor triggers co-opt existing language circuitry rather than forming isolated circuits, as shown by substantial overlap between trigger-activated attention heads and natural language heads across model scales.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that backdoor triggers hijack existing language circuitry, which has implications for interpretability-informed backdoor detection and mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Trigger information forms in early layers (7.5-25% of model depth).
Trigger-activated heads substantially overlap with heads naturally encoding output language.
The overlap is consistent across model scales (1B, 8B, 24B).
Some trigger-activated heads are shared across French and German triggers, suggesting a common trigger-processing mechanism.
Language representation is shared across target languages (French, German, Italian, Spanish).
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to language-switching triggers in the GAPperon model family; other backdoor types or architectures may operate differently.
Methodological choices, such as the top 10 heads threshold and use of Jaccard index, may affect overlap estimates and do not establish complete causal mechanisms.
Language coverage is limited to Latin script languages; generalization to languages with different writing systems is untested.
future_direction: Verifying causal necessity by ablating the identified heads.
Generalization to other model architectures or trigger injection methods.
Testing on languages with different writing systems.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose significant security risks for Large Language Models (LLMs), yet the internal mechanisms by which triggers operate remain poorly understood. We present the first mechanistic analysis of language-switching backdoors, studying the GAPperon model family (1B, 8B, 24B parameters) which contains triggers injected during pretraining that cause output language switching. Using activation patching, we localize trigger formation to early layers (7.5-25% of model depth) and identify which attention heads process trigger information. Our central finding is that trigger-activated heads substantially overlap with heads naturally encoding output language across model scales, with Jaccard indices between 0.18 and 0.66 over the top heads identified. This suggests that backdoor triggers do not form isolated circuits but instead co-opt the model's existing language components. These findings have implications for backdoor defense: detection methods may benefit from monitoring known functional components rather than searching for hidden circuits, and mitigation strategies could potentially leverage this entanglement between injected and natural behaviors.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: HiddenDetect: Detecting Jailbreak Attacks against Large Vision-Language Models via Monitoring Hidden States
papers.research_question: Can LVLMs detect unsafe prompts through their internal hidden states before generating any output? The paper investigates whether LVLMs inherently encode safety-relevant signals within their internal activations during inference.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces HiddenDetect, a tuning-free framework that detects jailbreak attacks by monitoring refusal semantics in the hidden states of LVLMs, and shows that LVLMs exhibit distinct activation patterns for unsafe prompts.
papers.conclusion: HiddenDetect leverages intrinsic safety signals in LVLM activations to detect jailbreak attacks without tuning, outperforming existing methods and offering a robust and scalable solution for enhancing LVLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
LVLMs exhibit distinct activation patterns when processing unsafe prompts, with refusal semantics detectable in hidden states.
Safety activation is delayed for multimodal inputs, especially when harmful intent is conveyed through images, correlating with higher attack success rates.
HiddenDetect achieves higher AUROC than existing state-of-the-art methods on both text-based and multimodal jailbreak benchmarks.
The method is tuning-free, operates directly on internal activations, and generalizes across different LVLM architectures without modification.
The most safety-aware layers are in the middle to late range, and scaling their weights increases the rejection of malicious queries.
papers.limitation:
Relies on the assumption that unsafe prompts consistently induce distinct activation patterns, which may not hold for all adversarial inputs.
Does not actively intervene in response generation, only flags unsafe prompts.
future_direction: Explore adaptive learning mechanisms to dynamically refine detection thresholds.
Integrate activation-based safety monitoring with controlled response modulation.
papers.abstract: The integration of additional modalities increases the susceptibility of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to safety risks, such as jailbreak attacks, compared to their language-only counterparts. While existing research primarily focuses on post-hoc alignment techniques, the underlying safety mechanisms within LVLMs remain largely unexplored. In this work , we investigate whether LVLMs inherently encode safety-relevant signals within their internal activations during inference. Our findings reveal that LVLMs exhibit distinct activation patterns when processing unsafe prompts, which can be leveraged to detect and mitigate adversarial inputs without requiring extensive fine-tuning. Building on this insight, we introduce HiddenDetect, a novel tuning-free framework that harnesses internal model activations to enhance safety. Experimental results show that {HiddenDetect} surpasses state-of-the-art methods in detecting jailbreak attacks against LVLMs. By utilizing intrinsic safety-aware patterns, our method provides an efficient and scalable solution for strengthening LVLM robustness against multimodal threats. Our code will be released publicly at https://github.com/leigest519/HiddenDetect.

papers.title: Attributing and Exploiting Safety Vectors through Global Optimization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can safety-critical attention heads in Large Language Models be identified through global optimization that accounts for cooperative interactions between components, and what does this reveal about the underlying safety mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GOSV, a global optimization framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads in LLMs, revealing two distinct sets of safety vectors (Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors) with low overlap, indicating separate functional pathways for safety. Based on these insights, the authors develop an inference-time jailbreak attack that outperforms existing white-box methods.
papers.conclusion: Aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety mechanisms, encoded in approximately 30% of attention heads. The GOSV framework advances mechanistic understanding of LLM safety and reveals fundamental vulnerabilities in current alignment approaches.
papers.key_findings:
GOSV identifies two spatially distinct sets of safety-critical attention heads (Malicious Injection Vectors via Harmful Patching and Safety Suppression Vectors via Zero Ablation) with consistently low overlap, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety.
Complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30% of total attention heads are repatched across all tested models, indicating that safety mechanisms are encoded in a distributed subset comprising roughly one-third of attention heads.
An inference-time jailbreak attack that repatches activations at the identified safety-critical heads achieves superior Attack Success Rates compared to existing white-box attacks, validating the effectiveness of the discovered safety vectors.
The two repatching strategies (Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation) target largely disjoint sets of attention heads, supporting the existence of distinct safety pathways rather than a unified mechanism.
Progressive intervention analysis shows that model behavior transitions from complete refusal to full harmful compliance as the number of repatched heads approaches the 30% threshold, with further intervention leading to degraded language capabilities.
papers.limitation:
No defense strategies have been developed to mitigate the identified vulnerabilities.
The approach requires white-box access for activation patching, limiting applicability to black-box scenarios.
Evaluation is limited to a set of open-source models and English-language instructions; generalizability to larger proprietary models, multilingual contexts, and other safety-critical behaviors requires further investigation.
future_direction: Developing robust safeguards based on the insights from GOSV.
Extending the approach to black-box scenarios.
Investigating generalizability to larger proprietary models, multilingual contexts, and other safety-critical behaviors.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to mitigate risks, their safety guardrails remain fragile against jailbreak attacks. This reveals limited understanding of components governing safety. Existing methods rely on local, greedy attribution that assumes independent component contributions. However, they overlook the cooperative interactions between different components in LLMs, such as attention heads, which jointly contribute to safety mechanisms. We propose \textbf{G}lobal \textbf{O}ptimization for \textbf{S}afety \textbf{V}ector Extraction (GOSV), a framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads through global optimization over all heads simultaneously. We employ two complementary activation repatching strategies: Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation. These strategies identify two spatially distinct sets of safety vectors with consistently low overlap, termed Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety purposes. Through systematic analyses, we find that complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30\% of total heads are repatched across all models. Building on these insights, we develop a novel inference-time white-box jailbreak method that exploits the identified safety vectors through activation repatching. Our attack substantially outperforms existing white-box attacks across all test models, providing strong evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed GOSV framework on LLM safety interpretability.

papers.title: TRYLOCK: Defense-in-Depth Against LLM Jailbreaks via Layered Preference and Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can a defense-in-depth architecture combining weight-level, activation-level, and input-level mechanisms protect LLMs against jailbreak attacks while maintaining usability?
papers.core_contribution: TRYLOCK is a defense-in-depth architecture that combines DPO safety training, RepE activation steering, adaptive sidecar classification, and input canonicalization, achieving an 88.0% relative reduction in Attack Success Rate while reducing over-refusal through adaptive steering.
papers.conclusion: Defense-in-depth with multiple complementary mechanisms (weight modification, activation steering, input classification, and canonicalization) is an effective approach for robust LLM safety against jailbreak attacks, though a trade-off between security and usability remains.
papers.key_findings:
The layered defense reduces Attack Success Rate from 46.5% to 5.6% (88.0% relative reduction) on a 249-prompt attack set.
Each defense layer provides complementary coverage: RepE blocks 36% of attacks that bypass DPO alone, and canonicalization catches 14% of encoding attacks that evade both.
A non-monotonic steering phenomenon was discovered where intermediate steering strength (α=1.0) degrades safety below the DPO-only baseline.
Adaptive steering via a sidecar classifier reduces over-refusal from 60% (fixed α=2.0) to 48% while maintaining identical attack defense.
The defense generalizes to the held-out JailbreakBench, achieving 78.8% relative ASR reduction (52.0% to 11.0%).
papers.limitation:
Evaluation set size and representativeness: the 50-prompt benign set yields wide confidence intervals for over-refusal, and larger diverse evaluations are needed.
Sidecar classifier errors: 18% of attacks are misclassified as SAFE, receiving minimal steering and resulting in higher ASR for those attacks.
future_direction: Extend TRYLOCK to additional base models, non-English languages, and integration with standard LLM serving frameworks.
Improve the sidecar classifier calibration and explore ensemble classifiers for better attack detection.
Conduct larger and more diverse benign evaluations to better characterize usability impact.
papers.abstract: Large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, and single-layer defenses often trade security for usability. We present TRYLOCK, the first defense-in-depth architecture that combines four heterogeneous mechanisms across the inference stack: weight-level safety alignment via DPO, activation-level control via Representation Engineering (RepE) steering, adaptive steering strength selected by a lightweight sidecar classifier, and input canonicalization to neutralize encoding-based bypasses. On Mistral-7B-Instruct evaluated against a 249-prompt attack set spanning five attack families, TRYLOCK achieves 88.0% relative ASR reduction (46.5% to 5.6%), with each layer contributing unique coverage: RepE blocks 36% of attacks that bypass DPO alone, while canonicalization catches 14% of encoding attacks that evade both. We discover a non-monotonic steering phenomenon -- intermediate strength (alpha=1.0) degrades safety below baseline -- and provide mechanistic hypotheses explaining RepE-DPO interference. The adaptive sidecar reduces over-refusal from 60% to 48% while maintaining identical attack defense, demonstrating that security and usability need not be mutually exclusive. We release all components -- trained adapters, steering vectors, sidecar classifier, preference pairs, and complete evaluation methodology -- enabling full reproducibility.

papers.title: NLSR: Neuron-Level Safety Realignment of Large Language Models Against Harmful Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we restore the safety of large language models after harmful fine-tuning without requiring additional training, by focusing on neuron-level updates?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free, neuron-level safety realignment framework that restores model safety by identifying and patching safety-critical neurons based on similarity differences before and after fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Neuron-level safety realignment is an effective, training-free approach to restore safety in LLMs after harmful fine-tuning, without disrupting the task-specific optimization process.
papers.key_findings:
NLSR effectively restores safety in fine-tuned models across multiple downstream tasks while maintaining task-level accuracy.
Safety-critical neurons show noticeable similarity differences after fine-tuning, which can be corrected by transplanting neurons from a reference model.
Adaptive safety-critical layer pruning is necessary for identifying safety-compromised layers.
After safety pre-amplification, various safety neuron identification methods (Wanda, SNIP, and the proposed method) show high similarity in localizing safety-critical neurons.
The method is decoupled from the fine-tuning phase and requires no additional training.
papers.abstract: The emergence of finetuning-as-a-service has revealed a new vulnerability in large language models (LLMs). A mere handful of malicious data uploaded by users can subtly manipulate the finetuning process, resulting in an alignment-broken model. Existing methods to counteract fine-tuning attacks typically require substantial computational resources. Even with parameter-efficient techniques like LoRA, gradient updates remain essential. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{N}euron-\textbf{L}evel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{R}ealignment (\textbf{NLSR}), a training-free framework that restores the safety of LLMs based on the similarity difference of safety-critical neurons before and after fine-tuning. The core of our framework is first to construct a safety reference model from an initially aligned model to amplify safety-related features in neurons. We then utilize this reference model to identify safety-critical neurons, which we prepare as patches. Finally, we selectively restore only those neurons that exhibit significant similarity differences by transplanting these prepared patches, thereby minimally altering the fine-tuned model. Extensive experiments demonstrate significant safety enhancements in fine-tuned models across multiple downstream tasks, while greatly maintaining task-level accuracy. Our findings suggest regions of some safety-critical neurons show noticeable differences after fine-tuning, which can be effectively corrected by transplanting neurons from the reference model without requiring additional training. The code will be available at \url{https://github.com/xinykou/NLSR}

papers.title: Learning Safety Constraints for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we learn and enforce safety constraints in large language models via a geometric polytope in the model's representation space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SaP, a geometric framework that learns safety constraints as a polytope in the LLM's representation space, enabling post-hoc safety steering and interpretable insights into safety concepts.
papers.conclusion: The geometric perspective of safety constraints offers a promising framework for aligning and controlling model behaviors, though further research is needed for theoretical foundations and robustness.
papers.key_findings:
SaP effectively defends against adversarial attacks while preserving model capabilities on standard benchmarks.
The learned polytope facets naturally correspond to different semantic safety concepts (e.g., violence, misinformation).
The concept encoder reduces polysemanticity in the learned features, improving interpretability and defense performance.
SaP's geometric approach provides a more structured and effective safety model compared to MLP-based classifiers.
The method operates post-hoc without model fine-tuning, preserving original model weights.
papers.limitation:
The heuristic facet assignment algorithm limits overall performance.
Under many attacks, specifically for the Ministral-8B model, SaP can induce semantically incoherent outputs.
Lacks a rigorous theoretical understanding and formal guarantees for safety in large-scale models.
future_direction: Further disentangling semantic understandings across polytope edges, possibly using mechanistic interpretability or non-linear geometric representations.
Improving SaP's performance in adversarial robustness and broad capability domains.
